- **Town centre (local DM60): CONFLICT.** "the principal impact would be the loss of the retail premises in a location wholly appropriate for such continued use" (DL ¶10).
- **Heritage, HE5(2): HARM, low end.** "The loss of the retail unit, in principle, therefore, undermines the significance of the GWCA in this location" (DL ¶18). "I find the proposal would harm the significance of the GWCA as a whole, albeit that this would be at the low end of the scale" (DL ¶19).
- **HE6(4) and HE4(2): FAIL.** "I am not persuaded that the public benefits would be of sufficient magnitude to outweigh the harm to the significance of the heritage asset, and the considerable importance this carries. Therefore, the harm that would be caused to the significance of the GWCA lacks clear and convincing justification" (DL ¶24).
- **Fallback (Class MA): limited weight.** "this has not been secured and there is therefore no more than a theoretical possibility that development might take place" (DL ¶28).
- **TC2 benefit: limited.** "As such, the benefits to the vitality and viability of the town centre would be limited" (DL ¶33).
- **DP3(1) and DP3(3).** "Policy DP3.3 requires substantial weight to be given to compliance with relevant development plan policies in relation to design quality and proposals should be refused where they lack clear justification for non-compliance in this respect" (DL ¶34).

## Planning balance
HE6(4) first (DL ¶21–24), then the development plan (DL ¶31), then S4(1). "Taken together, I find the benefits of the proposal would be substantially outweighed by its adverse effects" (DL ¶35). TC2 and L2 are named as substantial-weight benefits but both are discounted on the facts: no net gain in homes, and a unit vacant only a short time. DP3(3) is paraphrased with its clear-justification test and used as a weight in the S4 balance; no separate finding on justification is made for the design conflict.

## What made the difference
The street was fully let apart from this unit, which had been empty only a few months after a 10-year tenancy. That undercut both the vitality case and the L2 vacant-building benefit. With no extra dwelling, there was little on the other side of the heritage balance.

## Transferable points
- In a conservation area whose significance lies in ground-floor commercial activity, losing the retail use is itself heritage harm, apart from the design of the new frontage (DL ¶18).
- TC2 substantial weight for residential use in a town centre is cut to limited where there is no net gain in dwellings and a retail unit is lost (DL ¶33).
- L2 weight for reusing a vacant building depends on evidence that it is not attractive to the market; a short vacancy does not show that (DL ¶33).
- A Class MA fallback needs prior approval to be more than "a theoretical possibility" (DL ¶28).
- Emerging plan policies that are not put before the inspector get limited weight under DM4 (DL ¶3).
- Low-end harm to a conservation area beat a scheme with limited public benefits (DL ¶19, ¶24).
PINS-6010392:
## Summary
A larger replacement house on a wide Green Belt plot in a linear street at Stanton on the Wolds. The parties agreed it was not inappropriate under GB7(1)(e). The only issue was character: the scheme exceeded the volume limit in the Council's Design Code Supplementary Planning Document (SPD), but the inspector found no harm and declined to apply the limit rigidly. Allowed. The self-build status, needed for the biodiversity net gain exemption, was secured by a negatively worded condition requiring a planning obligation.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I am satisfied that the parts of the Framework most relevant to this appeal have not substantively changed from the previous iteration and therefore I have not sought comments from the main parties" (DL ¶2).
- **Green Belt, GB7(1)(e): PASS (agreed).** "The main parties agree that, with reference to what is now Policy GB7.1.e of the Framework (previously paragraph 154g)), the proposed development is not inappropriate development in the Green Belt" (DL ¶3).
- **Design standard not applied rigidly.** "The SPD sets out the expectations for new development, but there will be occasions where the application of its policies may not be necessary or beneficial to a given development proposal" (DL ¶6). "I do not consider it appropriate or necessary in this instance to impose such rigid restrictions on the proposed development as those contained within the SPD" (DL ¶7).
- **Character: NO HARM.** "the size and height of the proposed dwelling would fail to meet the stipulations of Policy C6.6 of the SPD. However, in this instance, this would not result in harm to the character and appearance of the area" (DL ¶9).
- **S3, S4 and S5.** "The main parties agree that the appeal proposal represents the redevelopment of previously developed land. It therefore benefits from part 1.d of Policy S5" (DL ¶13). "The proposal therefore would accord with whichever Framework policy were to be applied" (DL ¶14).
- **Self-build and biodiversity net gain.** "This is to my mind an exceptional circumstance, because the securing of self-build means that the proposed development is exempted from statutory Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG)" (DL ¶21). "The imposition of a negatively-worded condition requiring the submission of a planning obligation (14) secures this benefit, in the exceptional circumstances that I have set out" (DL ¶22).

## Planning balance
No harm was found, so there was nothing to weigh. The letter applies S5(1)(d) to a Green Belt site and leaves open whether S4 or S5 applies; it does not mention S5(5), which sends Green Belt proposals to GB6 to GB8. Because GB7(1)(e) was agreed and no adverse effect was found, the route makes no difference to the result.

## What made the difference
The plot and the street. A double-width plot, a deep set-back and a varied street of large dwellings meant the extra volume caused no harm, so the numerical limit in the SPD had no work to do.

## Transferable points
- A design code SPD limit (50% volume for replacement dwellings) is an expectation, not a rule: breach without harm is not a design conflict (DL ¶6–9).
- A missing self-build obligation was cured by a negatively worded condition requiring a planning obligation before commencement, as an "exceptional circumstance" tied to the removal of the self-build exemption on 6 August 2026 (DL ¶20–22). Most appeals treat a missing obligation as fatal.
- The inspector doubted that self-build can be secured by an ordinary condition because of the difficulty of enforcing occupation by the builder (DL ¶19).
- A council that suggests conditions must give reasons; under DM6, conditions with no stated basis, and removal of permitted development rights without clear justification, are not imposed (DL ¶15, ¶23).
- GB7(1)(e) for a replacement dwelling was accepted on the parties' agreement with no openness finding (DL ¶3).
PINS-6010578:
## Summary
Permission in principle for 5 homes on Green Belt land at Monks Heath, outside any settlement. Grey belt and unmet need were agreed. The contest was the sustainable location limb, which the inspector passed: a bus stop about 391 m away with two staggered hourly services, a range of services within about 500 m, and a usable footpath separated from the road by a verge, though uneven and mostly unlit. A Connectivity Tool score of 33 was treated as above average for this type of location. The scheme was not inappropriate and was allowed under S5(5).

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties were provided with an opportunity to comment. I have had regard to the 2026 version of the Framework in my decision" (DL ¶7).
- **Grey belt, GB7(1)(g)(i): PASS (agreed).** "the main parties do not dispute that the site would meet the definition of grey belt land and that the proposal would not undermine the purposes of the remaining Green Belt" (DL ¶11).
- **Unmet need, GB7(1)(g)(ii): PASS (agreed).** "there is no dispute between the parties that the Council cannot demonstrate a 5-year supply of deliverable housing land" (DL ¶12).
- **Sustainable location, GB7(1)(g)(iii) / TR3: PASS.** "the footpath remains generally usable and is separated from the carriageway by a substantial grass verge" (DL ¶14). "although each service operates hourly, their staggered timetables provide more frequent opportunities for travel throughout the day including during key commuting periods" (DL ¶15). "Although future occupiers would be likely to make some use of the private car for day-to-day journeys, the evidence indicates that there remains a genuine and realistic choice of transport modes" (DL ¶25).
- **Connectivity Tool, TR3(2).** "This represents an above average result for a site in this type of location" (DL ¶18).
- **Reduced mobility.** Concerns about wheelchair users and others with reduced mobility were answered by reference to the site's semi-rural context: "I am not convinced that the condition of the local footpaths along renders the location unsustainable" (DL ¶24).
- **GB7 categories are alternatives.** "where a development falls within any of the exceptions of Policy GB7, there is no requirement to demonstrate that any of the other exceptions within the Framework would also be met, such as that under Policy GB7(1)(h)" (DL ¶22).
- **Openness not re-assessed.** "there is no place for a subsequent assessment of the effect of the development on the openness of the Green Belt" (DL ¶21).
- **Flood risk, F5: PASS at PIP stage.** "the evidence before me does not suggest that the areas affected by surface water flooding would, in principle, prevent the site from accommodating 5 dwellings" (DL ¶30).

## Planning balance
S5(5), applying S5(2). "Policy S5(5) of the Framework indicates that, through the application of Policy GB7, proposals should be approved unless the benefits of doing so would be substantially outweighed by any adverse effects when assessed against the national decision-making policies in the Framework and applying paragraph S5(2)" (DL ¶33). No adverse effects were found; the benefits (homes in a shortfall, construction and occupation spending) "are not outweighed by any adverse effects" (DL ¶34). No weight word is given to the housing.

## What made the difference
A footway for the whole route, kept apart from the traffic by a verge, and timetable evidence for two bus services at a stop under 400 m away. With services within 500 m, the lack of lighting and the uneven surface did not defeat the location. The Connectivity Tool score was low in absolute terms (33) but was judged against scores for nearby approved schemes.

## Transferable points
- Limb (iii) passed on a mostly unlit but continuous footpath separated from the carriageway, plus two evidenced hourly bus services with staggered times (DL ¶14–15, ¶18).
- A Connectivity Tool score is read against comparators: 33 was "above average" for the type of location and in line with 29 to 34 at nearby approved schemes (DL ¶18).
- The inspector discounted a concern about wheelchair users because of the semi-rural context (DL ¶24). That reasoning is open to challenge: TR3(1) refers to good accessibility for different users.
- A highway officer's accessibility concerns that stop short of an objection in principle did not prevent a pass (DL ¶25).
- One GB7 category is enough; GB7(1)(h) need not also be shown (DL ¶22).
- At PIP stage, surface water risk on part of a site is left to technical details where the amount of development can avoid it (DL ¶30).
- After a not-inappropriate finding, S5(5) is applied together with S5(2) (DL ¶33).
PINS-6010746:
## Summary
A much larger replacement house in the Green Belt at Matching. It failed the replacement-building category GB7(1)(b) as materially larger (floorspace up 141.9%), but passed GB7(1)(e): the plot is previously developed land and the harm to openness was moderate, not substantial. So it was not inappropriate. It was still dismissed, because its scale and urban design caused low harm to the setting of a Grade II listed thatched house nearby with no public benefits to weigh against it, and harmed the rural character of the row.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "the parties have been provided with an opportunity to comment on the revised Framework" (DL ¶2).
- **GB7(1)(b) replacement: FAIL.** "Taken together, the new building would be materially larger than the one it would replace" (DL ¶8).
- **GB7(1)(e) previously developed land: PASS.** "the site would be previously developed land and the proposal for a replacement detached dwelling would comprise a redevelopment" (DL ¶10). "Given that the proposal would not cause substantial harm to the openness of the Green Belt, the development would accord with criterion e of Policy GB7 of the Framework" (DL ¶15).
- **Not inappropriate.** "Therefore, the proposal is not inappropriate development, as per Policy GB7 of the Framework" (DL ¶16).
- **Heritage, HE5(2) degree of harm.** "The proposal would result in a low degree of harm, given the limited contribution that the appeal site makes to the significance of Inglenook" (DL ¶21).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "there is no substantive evidence before me that demonstrates the existing dwelling could not achieve a similar level of living and energy standards and accessibility" (DL ¶23). "public benefits would not outweigh the harm identified" (DL ¶23).
- **HE6(1) and HE6(3).** "Whilst the level of harm is at the lower level, Policy HE6 states that any harm to a designated heritage asset will be a matter of considerable importance and weight and that substantial weight should be given to the asset’s conservation" (DL ¶30).
- **Character: CONFLICT (local DM9).** "its scale and overtly urban design would fail to reflect the prevailing scale and prevailing rural character of the area" (DL ¶27).
- **Fallback: limited weight.** No "substantive details, including plans or a Lawful Development Certificate" (DL ¶31).

## Planning balance
Plan-led (s38(6)), after HE6(4). "The Framework does not change the statutory status of the development plan as the starting point for decision making" (DL ¶29). Limited benefits against low heritage harm, character harm and plan conflict (DL ¶33). The letter does not run the S5(5) "substantially outweighed" balance that follows a not-inappropriate finding; with HE6(4) failed, the result would be the same.

## What made the difference
Passing the Green Belt test did not save the scheme. The same bulk that made it "materially larger" harmed the listed building's rural setting, and a one-for-one replacement has no housing benefit to put in the HE6(4) balance.

## Transferable points
- GB7 categories are alternatives: a replacement dwelling that fails (b) as materially larger can pass (e) as redevelopment of previously developed land if openness harm is below substantial (DL ¶8, ¶15–16).
- A residential plot outside a built-up area is previously developed land; the garden exclusion applies only in built-up areas (DL ¶10).
- A 141.9% floorspace increase caused "moderate" openness harm, which is not "substantial harm" under (e) (DL ¶7, ¶15).
- A one-for-one replacement has no housing-supply benefit for HE6(4); energy and accessibility gains count only if the existing building could not achieve them (DL ¶23).
- Low harm to a Grade II setting beat a single replacement dwelling (DL ¶21, ¶30, ¶33).
- A permitted development fallback needs plans or a lawful development certificate to show a realistic prospect (DL ¶31).
PINS-6010933:
## Summary
A timber cabin for printmaking, joinery and boat repair on a boat storage plot just outside Brightlingsea, in the local Coastal Protection Belt. The inspector found a compelling functional requirement for the coastal location, no harm to character, highway safety or the nearby conservation area, and support from E2 and L2(1)(b). The scheme accorded with the development plan and was allowed with conditions limiting the use. S5 was not applied although the site is outside the settlement boundary.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "Annex A, Paragraph 1 states that this version of the Framework applies to decision-making from the day of its publication, therefore references to the Framework in this decision are to the August 2026 version" (DL ¶4).
- **Coastal Protection Belt (local PPL 2): ACCORD.** "in the absence of a specific definition of what is meant by “compelling functional or operational requirement”, I find that the proposal would provide a compelling functional requirement to be located within the Coastal Protection Belt" (DL ¶10).
- **Fallback.** "I consider that the fallback position would be noticeably more harmful to the character and appearance of the area due to these differences" (DL ¶14). "Therefore, the fallback position would have moderate weight in my decision insofar as it relates to character and appearance" (DL ¶14).
- **Design, DP3(1) and DP3(2): ACCORD.** "The proposal would also accord with Policies DP3(1) and DP3(2) of the Framework" (DL ¶17).
- **Highway safety: ACCORD.** "It would also accord with Policies TR3 and TR4 of the Framework, which, taken together, seek to prevent adverse impacts on highway safety and minimise the scope for conflict between pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles" (DL ¶22).
- **Conservation area, HE5(2): NO EFFECT.** "I consider that the proposal would have no effect on the significance of the CA" (DL ¶24).
- **Economic benefits.** "This accords with Policy E2 of the Framework which states that substantial weight should be given to economic benefits of proposals for commercial development which allow businesses to invest, expand and/or adapt" (DL ¶30).
- **Conditions, DM6(2)(c).** "Policy DM6(2)(c) of the Framework states that conditions should not be used to restrict national permitted development rights unless there is clear justification to do so" (DL ¶32).

## Planning balance
Plan-led. "The proposal would be in accordance with the development plan as a whole. Material considerations do not indicate a decision should be taken other than in accordance with the development plan" (DL ¶36). No S5(1) category is identified for a site outside the settlement boundary, and no S5 balance is run; with no harm found, nothing turned on it.

## What made the difference
The marine link. The activities taken together served the boat storage use, which met the local policy's functional test, and the cabin was hidden by vegetation. The extant permission for a taller B8 cabin made the built form a non-issue.

## Transferable points
- A fallback can carry different weights for different issues: very limited on use (no evidence the B8 cabin would be less intensive), moderate on character (it would be more harmful) (DL ¶11, ¶14).
- HE5(2) outcomes are used as the finding: "no effect" on a conservation area ends the heritage analysis (DL ¶23–24).
- DM6(2)(c) needs clear justification to remove permitted development rights; a locational policy requiring a functional need for the specific use supplied it (DL ¶32).
- E2 and L2(1)(b) substantial weight were applied to a single small workshop cabin (DL ¶30).
PINS-6011060:
## Summary
Prior approval for a telecommunications mast in a protected woodland belt beside parkland that serves as Suitable Alternative Natural Greenspace (SANG). The inspector found a significant adverse effect from siting and appearance and no information on the protected trees. Substantial weight to network benefits under CO1 was acknowledged, but the CO2(1)(b) evidence on alternative sites was too thin. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "the parties have been provided with an opportunity to comment on the revised Framework" (DL ¶4).
- **Siting and appearance: HARM.** "It would rise above the tree canopy with an engineered form that would appear out of place in a naturalistic setting" (DL ¶9).
- **SANG.** "The SANG is a strategic ecological mitigation asset, and the erosion of its quality could mean that it is less able to fulfil its intended function" (DL ¶13).
- **Alternatives, CO2(1)(b): FAIL.** "Policy CO2 1. b. of the Framework requires evidence that, where a new site is proposed, the applicant has sought to keep the number of new sites to a minimum and has explored the possibility of erecting antennas on an existing building, mast or other structure" (DL ¶21). "Several other sites are discounted because of an unwilling landowner. Whilst this does present a considerable constraint, it is not one that is unsurmountable" (DL ¶23).
- **CO1 weight.** "the clear and persuasive evidence regarding the unsuitability of alternative sites is not before me and I cannot therefore conclude that alternative sites have been thoroughly considered" (DL ¶26).

## What made the difference
The alternatives evidence. Two nearby sites outside the Tree Preservation Order and the SANG were dismissed by the appellant for reasons the inspector could not follow, and the appellant said it was working on a different solution. With significant visual harm and no tree evidence, CO1's substantial weight was not enough.

## Transferable points
- CO1 substantial weight does not carry a mast where CO2(1)(b) evidence on alternatives is brief and unexplained (DL ¶21–26).
- An unwilling landowner does not by that fact rule out an alternative site (DL ¶23).
- Harm to a SANG's attractiveness carries more weight than harm to ordinary open space because of its role in protecting a Special Protection Area (DL ¶13).
- Effects on Tree Preservation Order woodland are part of siting and appearance and cannot be deferred to a tree works application (DL ¶16).
PINS-6011081:
## Summary
Two studio flats over a car wash waiting area behind shops on Barking Road, East Ham. The inspector found harm to the Aintree Avenue street scene, poor living conditions for future occupiers and neighbours, and no workable cycle or waste storage. Housing and effective use of land got substantial weight despite the small scale, but the design conflict with DP3 (which the letter calls "D3") was treated as a "should be refused" policy, and under S4 the benefits were substantially outweighed. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** A revised Framework "replaces previous iterations, and the contents of which have been considered in the determination of this appeal" (DL ¶4).
- **Character, DP3(1): CONFLICT.** "It would therefore appear as an incongruous addition to the street scene" (DL ¶9).
- **Future occupiers, P3: CONFLICT.** "Framework Policy P3 requires development proposals to, amongst other things, provide healthy living conditions for occupiers" (DL ¶13). "the future residents of Flat 1 would be afforded a poor and oppressive outlook from their single window" (DL ¶14).
- **Neighbours: CONFLICT.** "the proximity of the proposal and its two-storey height would create an overwhelming sense of enclosure and oppressive environment for the residents of No 239A" (DL ¶21).
- **Benefits: substantial.** "Therefore, these benefits attract substantial weight, despite its small scale" (DL ¶25).
- **DP3(3) trigger.** "the proposal would be in fundamental conflict with Framework Policy D3 relating to character and appearance that stipulates permission should be refused in such circumstances" (DL ¶28).

## Planning balance
S4(1). "The appeal site is located within a settlement and therefore Framework Policy S4 is engaged. In this case, given the conflict with Policy D3, the benefits of the proposal would be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶29). The design conflict alone carries the balance against benefits given substantial weight. The letter does not ask whether there is "clear justification" and does not cite S4(2)(c), but uses DP3(3) in the way S4(2)(c) describes. "Policy D3" at DL ¶28–29 is a slip for DP3: D3 is the London Plan design policy.

## What made the difference
A two-storey residential building squeezed onto a car wash yard 4.4 m from the windows of existing flats. Substantial weight to two homes and to the use of airspace did not help once the design conflict was treated as a refusal policy.

## Transferable points
- Substantial weight to housing and effective use of land (L2) "despite its small scale" is still substantially outweighed where DP3 says refuse (DL ¶25, ¶28–29).
- An inspector treated the DP3 refusal limb as decisive under S4 without naming S4(2)(c) or asking about clear justification (DL ¶28–29).
- Development plan design and amenity policies found "broadly consistent with the Framework" keep their weight (DL ¶8, ¶13, ¶19, ¶24).
- Living above a noisy existing use needs a noise assessment; an unassessed risk counts against the scheme (DL ¶16).
PINS-6011302:
## Summary
A former car sales premises in Nottingham had been split into two units focused on vehicle repairs and servicing, one sharing a party wall with a house. The appellant's own noise assessment showed a significant impact and offered no mitigation for noise and vibration through the wall. The inspector ran the S4 balance: a small economic benefit under E2 was substantially outweighed by the P3 harm, and P4 gave no support because the uses were not lawful. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "Those parts of the Framework most relevant to this appeal have been amended. As a result, parties have been provided with an opportunity to make further submissions" (DL ¶4).
- **Living conditions, P3: CONFLICT, significant weight.** "the noise assessment has failed to demonstrate that mitigation would satisfactorily address the impact on the occupiers of the adjoining property" (DL ¶12). "The scheme has an unacceptable adverse impact on the living conditions of the occupiers of No.12 and consequently the development is not appropriate for its location, contrary to Policy P3 of the Framework" (DL ¶23).
- **P4 existing businesses: NOT ENGAGED.** "the business operations operating from each of the units do not have planning permission or a relevant lawful development certificate. Consequently, Policy P4 does not weigh in favour of this retrospective scheme" (DL ¶22).
- **E2: small weight.** "given the modest size of the units, a small amount of weight is attached to this benefit" (DL ¶21).

## Planning balance
S4(1), within a settlement. "Overall, the benefits of the scheme would be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects and the presumption in favour of sustainable development does not apply" (DL ¶24). No "should be refused" trigger was needed: significant weight to one P3 conflict outweighed a small E2 benefit.

## What made the difference
The party wall. Mitigation was designed for the houses opposite, and nothing addressed the attached house. The appellant's own evidence established the harm.

## Transferable points
- P4 protects "permitted operations of existing businesses"; an unauthorised use seeking retrospective permission cannot rely on it (DL ¶22).
- E2 weight depends on scale: jobs in two modest units got "a small amount of weight", not the substantial weight E2 can carry (DL ¶21).
- A single significant P3 harm can substantially outweigh small benefits under S4(1) without a refusal trigger (DL ¶23–24).
- Conditions that control hours and openings do not answer structure-borne noise through a party wall (DL ¶15).
PINS-6011365:
## Summary
Permission in principle for up to seven self-build homes on a field just north of Fowlmere's development framework. The inspector found future residents would depend on the car, that building in the gap between the village and outlying houses would be inherently harmful, and that best and most versatile land would be lost. The self-build need was undisputed but got only moderate weight because technical details consent was uncertain. Under S5 the harms substantially outweighed the benefits, and the site was not suitably related to the settlement. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I invited the main parties to comment on any implications of these for their cases and took their responses into account in reaching my decision" (DL ¶4).
- **Accessibility: FAIL (CC2; TR3 not named).** "the first 100m of the road to it lacks a footway" (DL ¶6). "the village has no shops and a poor bus service, limiting the advantage obtained" (DL ¶8). "I am satisfied that future residents would be likely to depend on the car for access to most services and facilities" (DL ¶10).
- **Character: CONFLICT.** "I am satisfied that the impact of developing this site would be inherently harmful, so that design and landscaping could only reduce harm to character and appearance" (DL ¶13).
- **DP3.** "Policy DP3 of the Framework requires proposals to be refused if they would not respond to their context, integrate with and enhance their surroundings" (DL ¶24). "I attach substantial weight to this conflict" (DL ¶24).
- **Self-build weight: moderate.** "it is not certain that TDC would ultimately be granted and that the proposal would therefore contribute to meeting that need. Consequently, I attach only moderate weight to this consideration" (DL ¶25).
- **S5(1)(j): FAIL.** "I have also found that the proposal would not be suitably related to a settlement and its need for access to services and facilities could not be accommodated by available infrastructure" (DL ¶28).
- **Plan weight (Annex A ¶2).** "in the context of this appeal, SCLP Policies S/2, S/7, HQ/1 and NH/2 are not materially inconsistent with the Framework and so should continue to be afforded significant weight" (DL ¶29).

## Planning balance
S5(1) "substantially outweighed" (DL ¶22, ¶28). Harms: location (CC2, significant), character (DP3, substantial), agricultural land (N2, moderate). Benefits: self-build homes (HO7, moderate), economic (modest). "The unsuitable location, likely harm to character and appearance and loss of agricultural land would substantially outweigh the benefits, despite the shortfall in self- and custom-build serviced plots" (DL ¶28). The letter runs the S5(1) balance before finding the (j) criteria unmet, and does not cite S5(4) or S5(2).

## What made the difference
A village with no shop and a poor bus service, a first 100 m with no footway, and a site that sits in a gap beyond the village, not within it. The inspector distinguished an allowed PIP in the same district because that site "infilled a frontage gap within the village" (DL ¶12). A footway and bus stop were offered, but better infrastructure to a village with few services gained little.

## Transferable points
- Offering a footway and bus stop does little where the destination village has no shop and a poor bus service (DL ¶8).
- A railway station "within cycling distance" does not help without evidence of service frequency and where the route is at the national speed limit and crosses a main road (DL ¶9).
- At PIP stage, landscape harm that is "inherently harmful" cannot be left to technical details (DL ¶13).
- PIP self-build weight was cut from substantial to moderate because technical details consent, and so delivery, is uncertain (DL ¶25).
- Countryside, design and location policies were kept at significant weight under Annex A ¶2 "in the context of this appeal", where the scheme met no S5(1) category (DL ¶29).
- Location harm was weighed under CC2, not TR3 (DL ¶23).
PINS-6011489:
## Summary
A small plot of Green Belt pasture near Hemel Hempstead was to be used for appointment-only outdoor wellbeing sessions, with a prefabricated office unit for consultations. The inspector accepted the use of the land as outdoor recreation under GB7(1)(f)(iii) but found the building was not an "appropriate facility" under (f)(iv): nothing showed it was needed for the outdoor use. The scheme was inappropriate, with added harm to highway safety and character, and very special circumstances were not shown. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties were given the opportunity to comment on this" (DL ¶1).
- **GB7(1)(f)(iii) use of land: PASS.** "I accept that use of the land for the purposes stated would be recreational, and this would be consistent with part iii of Policy GB7.1.f of the Framework" (DL ¶6).
- **GB7(1)(f)(iv) building: FAIL.** "I cannot see any reason why the provision of the proposed building is necessary to support those uses" (DL ¶6). "such activities do not depend on a Green Belt location and there is no robust evidence to explain how such consultations are connected to an outdoor recreation or sports use" (DL ¶6). "I consider the proposed building would not represent an appropriate facility for the use of the land for outdoor recreation" (DL ¶8).
- **Inappropriate.** "the development the subject of this appeal does not fall within a category set out in Policy GB7 of the Framework" (DL ¶9).
- **Highway safety: HARM (local plan), significant weight.** "With there being no robust evidence that adequate parking can be provided, I consider the proposals would be harmful to highway safety" (DL ¶11).
- **Character: HARM, moderate weight** (DL ¶12).

## Planning balance
GB6(2) very special circumstances. Substantial weight to Green Belt harm, significant weight to highway safety harm and moderate weight to character harm, against little or very little weight to the therapeutic benefit, the operating controls and reversibility. "I do not consider the matters raised in support of the proposal to clearly outweigh the harm identified" (DL ¶18).

## What made the difference
The building, not the use. The outdoor activity was accepted as recreation. The office unit failed because consultations could happen anywhere and it filled much of a very small plot. Evidence tying a smaller shelter to the safe running of the outdoor sessions might have met (f)(iv).

## Transferable points
- The appropriate-facilities limb, GB7(1)(f)(iv), is read as a need test: the building must be shown to be necessary to support the outdoor use (DL ¶6, ¶8).
- An activity that does not depend on a Green Belt location (one-to-one consultations) does not make its building a facility for outdoor recreation (DL ¶6).
- A building that takes up a large part of a small site undermines the claim that the land is used for outdoor recreation (DL ¶7).
- Reversibility and a temporary permission do not make a building appropriate or remove its effect on openness (DL ¶14).
PINS-6011852:
## Summary
Retention for three years of a modern pergola in front of a Grade II listed villa used as a private hospital in Mill Hill. The inspector found that it competes with the balanced principal elevation and harms the building's significance through its setting. The benefits were private to users of the facility. Dismissed, as was the sister appeal for the rear pergola (PINS-6011855).

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "Whilst the format has altered, any considerations that are material to this decision have not fundamentally changed" (DL ¶5).
- **Harm: HE6(3).** "it disrupts the balanced composition and refined late Georgian proportions that underpin the building's special interest" (DL ¶10). "I therefore find that the proposal would result in harm to the significance of the designated heritage asset, to which I attach considerable importance and weight" (DL ¶11).
- **Public benefits: HE6(4) FAIL.** "such advantages are inherently private in nature and do not amount to public benefits in the heritage context" (DL ¶12).
- **Conflict.** "The development therefore conflicts with Framework Policy HE6" (DL ¶14).

## Planning balance
HE6(4): harm against public benefits, run before the development plan conclusion. The letter attributes the weighing to "Policy HE5" (DL ¶11); the weighing is in HE6(4), and the conclusion at DL ¶14 cites HE6. The slip is incidental.

## What made the difference
A conspicuous modern structure on the principal elevation of a listed villa, with no benefit to anyone but the facility's users.

## Transferable points
- Size and prominence that "compete with, rather than defer to, the host building" harm significance even with no effect on fabric (DL ¶10–11).
- Private benefits to users of a private healthcare facility do not count as public benefits under HE6(4) (DL ¶12).
PINS-6011855:
## Summary
Retention for three years of a modern pergola behind a Grade II listed villa used as a private hospital in Mill Hill. The inspector found harm to the building's significance through its setting, gave that harm considerable importance and weight, and held that comfort for patients and visitors is a private benefit, not a public one. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "Whilst the format has altered, any considerations that are material to this decision have not fundamentally changed" (DL ¶5).
- **Harm: HE6(3).** "I therefore find that the proposal would result in harm to the significance of the designated heritage asset, to which I attach considerable importance and weight" (DL ¶10). The degree of harm is not graded.
- **Public benefits: HE6(4) FAIL.** "such advantages are inherently private in nature and do not amount to public benefits in the heritage context" (DL ¶11).
- **Temporary permission.** "the temporary nature of the development attracts only limited weight and does not affect my overall conclusion on the proposal" (DL ¶12).
- **Conflict.** "The development therefore conflicts with Framework Policy HE6" (DL ¶13).

## Planning balance
HE6(4): harm against public benefits, run on its own terms before the development plan conclusion. The letter attributes the weighing to "Policy HE5" (DL ¶10); the weighing is in HE6(4), and the conclusion at DL ¶13 cites HE6. The slip is incidental.

## What made the difference
The benefits were all to users of a private facility, and part of the structure only sheltered plant and lockers. A three-year limit did not help because the harm would last the whole period.

## Transferable points
- Comfort and convenience for users of a private healthcare facility are private benefits and do not count in the HE6(4) balance (DL ¶11).
- A temporary permission does not reduce heritage harm while the structure stands; it attracted only limited weight (DL ¶12).
- A structure that does not touch listed fabric can still harm significance through the loss of open space in the setting (DL ¶10).
PINS-6012036:
## Summary
A 13 m amateur radio mast in the garden of a bungalow at Wroxall, in the setting of the Isle of Wight National Landscape. The inspector found significant harm to the street scene, more moderate harm to the setting of the National Landscape and an overbearing effect on neighbours. The letter runs the S4 balance, applies the S4(2)(c) "should be refused" trigger without naming the policy, and finds the benefits substantially outweighed. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The policy emphasis of the parts of the Framework most relevant to this appeal have not changed. As a result, I have not sought comments on the new version of the Framework" (DL ¶3).
- **New local plan.** "Appeal decisions must be based on the policies from the development plan prevailing at the time of determination" (DL ¶5).
- **Character and National Landscape setting: HARM.** "it would still create a very distinctive break in the skyline, forming an incongruous feature" (DL ¶11). "Although the harm to the setting of the NL would be at a more moderate level, I still attribute great weight to this harm" (DL ¶13).
- **Living conditions: CONFLICT.** "the installation would create a very close, dominant and overbearing feature, particularly to the immediate neighbouring bungalows" (DL ¶15).
- **Benefits.** "the evidence before me does not demonstrate that the proposal would facilitate significant public benefits in terms of its contribution towards community resilience, including emergency communications capability, and I afford this moderate weight in its favour" (DL ¶18).
- **Plan consistency.** "There is consistency between PS policies C1 and EV9, and national … policies DP3, N4 and L2" (DL ¶21; the … replaces "decision-making", which breaks across a line in the letter).
- **S4(2)(c) trigger.** "the proposal would fail to comply with one of the national … policies which state that development proposals should be refused in specific circumstances, as set out in policy S4(2)(c) of the Framework" (DL ¶22; the … again replaces "decision-making").

## Planning balance
S4(1), within a settlement. "I have found that the benefits of approving the appeal scheme would be substantially outweighed by adverse effects, when assessed against the national decision-making policies in the Framework. Consequently, the presumption in favour of sustainable development set out in policy S4 of the Framework does not apply" (DL ¶23). The "great weight" given to National Landscape harm (DL ¶9, ¶13) is the December 2024 wording; N4(1) of the 2026 Framework says "Substantial weight". The slip is incidental in a dismissal.

## What made the difference
Height and exposure: a mast well above the bungalow and the former railway line with nothing tall behind it, in gardens small enough that it dominated the neighbours. The claimed emergency communications benefit was asserted, not evidenced. A demountable pole was mentioned but was "not a determinative factor" (DL ¶19).

## Transferable points
- The S4(2)(c) trigger is applied to a domestic mast: design and landscape-setting harm is treated as failing a "should be refused" policy, though the letter does not say which one or ask whether there is clear justification (DL ¶21–22).
- A local plan adopted during the appeal replaces the policies cited in the refusal; the parties are asked to comment on the new plan (DL ¶4–5).
- Harm to the setting of a National Landscape "at a more moderate level" still attracted the highest weight the inspector applied (DL ¶13).
- Community resilience benefits of amateur radio need evidence of what the installation adds to existing capability (DL ¶18).
PINS-6012075:
## Summary
A freestanding electric vehicle charge point with two advertisement screens on the King's Road footway, opposite the Sloane/Stanley Conservation Area. The inspector found it incongruous in the street scene and harmful, at the lower level, to the conservation area through its setting. The charging benefits were modest and could be achieved less harmfully, so the HE6(4) balance failed. Highway safety was acceptable. Appeal A (planning) and the linked advertisement appeal were both dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties have been consulted and provided with an opportunity to provide comments on it in relation to these appeals" (DL ¶4).
- **Character: CONFLICT (local plan).** "it would have an undue presence in its setting, appearing as an incongruous and uncharacteristic feature" (DL ¶9).
- **Conservation area setting, HE6(4): FAIL.** "Whilst the degree of harm resulting from the proposed JOLT and advertisement on the significance of the CA would be at the lower level, in accordance with Policy HE6 (4) of the Framework, that harm should be weighed against any public benefits of the proposals" (DL ¶12). "I find insufficient public benefits arising from the proposals to offset the identified harm to which I attach substantial weight" (DL ¶14).
- **Less harmful alternative.** "these benefits would be modest and there is no indication that they could not be achieved in a less harmful manner than proposed" (DL ¶24).
- **Highway safety: PASS.** The unit "would not significantly interrupt any obvious desire line for pedestrians along the footpath" (DL ¶19).

## Planning balance
HE6(4): lower-level harm to a conservation area against modest public benefits from one charging unit. The inspector attached "substantial weight" to the harm (DL ¶14); the Framework gives substantial weight to the asset's conservation (HE6(1)) and treats harm as a matter of considerable importance and weight (HE6(3)). The slip is incidental: the weighing itself follows HE6(4). The appeal then fails against the development plan read as a whole (DL ¶25).

## What made the difference
The unit's size and solidity in a relatively open stretch of footway facing a conservation area, and the lack of any evidence that the charging benefits needed this design or this spot. At 369 Fulham Road the same inspector found no heritage harm, because the conservation area was 70 to 100 m away behind intervening buildings, but still dismissed on clutter and obstruction.

## Transferable points
- Electric vehicle charging is a public benefit, but one unit gives a modest benefit, and the HE6(4) balance asks whether it could be delivered in a less harmful way (DL ¶14, ¶24).
- Lower-level harm to a conservation area through its setting was enough to fail HE6(4) against a small infrastructure scheme (DL ¶12–14).
- A footway left at about 2 m, below a local 3 m standard but meeting Transport for London guidance, was acceptable where no desire line was interrupted (DL ¶18–19).
PINS-6012115:
## Summary
A static caravan let as a separate home, with its own access, on garden land in the Green Belt at St Leonards and St Ives. The inspector held that stationing a caravan as a home is not a change in the use of land of the kind GB7(1)(f)(iii) covers, and that the site fails the sustainable location limb of GB7(1)(g) because the walk to the A31 bus stops is long, mostly unlit and ends at an uncontrolled crossing. The scheme was inappropriate, and one small home did not amount to very special circumstances. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties were given the opportunity to comment, and the comments received have been taken into account in the determination of the appeal" (DL ¶2).
- **GB7(1)(f)(iii) change of use: FAIL.** "It is not an open-ended category but rather, because of the words “such as”, the uses that will be within it should take their flavour or extent from the examples given" (DL ¶9). "policy GB7(1)(f)(iii) does not include development that covers the provision of a static caravan" (DL ¶9).
- **GB7(1)(g)(iii) / TR3 sustainable location: FAIL.** "the distance along the pavement to Boundary Lane is a noticeable one, with most of its length being unlit" (DL ¶11). "these road conditions would not be an attractive option for walkers and those with mobility … issues, particularly during hours of darkness and in adverse weather" (DL ¶11; the … marks a page break). "the proposed development is not in a sustainable location, and as all the criteria listed must be satisfied, it would not fall under the category of development specified under policy GB7(1)(g) of the Framework" (DL ¶13).
- **Openness: HARM.** Moderate spatial harm and "moderate harm to visual openness" (DL ¶16–17).
- **Housing benefit: moderate.** "due to the small scale of the proposal, and thereby the small scale of the benefits, I afford this moderate weight" (DL ¶19).
- **Fallback: limited weight.** "the proposal would have a more harmful impact on the openness of the Green Belt than this fallback, and I afford this limited weight" (DL ¶20).

## Planning balance
GB6(2) very special circumstances. Substantial weight to Green Belt harm (inappropriateness plus moderate spatial and visual openness harm) against moderate weight to one home and limited weight to the fallback. "The other considerations in this case, as detailed above, do not have sufficient cumulative weight to clearly outweigh the harm to the Green Belt and any other harm" (DL ¶25). The letter then records: "For this reason, policy S5 of the Framework is not engaged" (DL ¶25).

## What made the difference
The route to the bus stops. The inspector did not need to decide grey belt or unmet need: limb (iii) failed on a long, mostly unlit pavement and an uncontrolled crossing of the A31, and all four limbs of (g) must be met. A lit route with a controlled crossing, or evidence of nearer services, would have been needed before the other limbs mattered.

## Transferable points
- GB7(1)(f)(iii) is read by its examples: "such as" outdoor sport, recreation and cemeteries gives the category its flavour, and stationing a caravan as a home is outside it (DL ¶9).
- A decision-maker can fail GB7(1)(g) on limb (iii) alone without deciding grey belt or unmet need (DL ¶13).
- A footway does not make a route acceptable where most of it is unlit and it ends at an uncontrolled crossing of a busy road; the route is judged for walkers and for people with mobility issues (DL ¶11).
- One home in the Green Belt: the Framework's substantial weight to providing homes was reduced to moderate for scale (DL ¶19).
- Once a scheme is inappropriate and very special circumstances are not shown, S5 "is not engaged" (DL ¶25).
PINS-6012289:
## Summary
Nine flats in three new storeys over a backland garage in Edgware, one storey more than an extant permission for seven flats. The inspector gave the fallback significant weight but found the fourth storey would make the building jarring in its transitional setting and overbearing for neighbours. Policy L2's substantial weight for airspace development was cut to little weight because the scheme was not consistent with the street scene. Under S4 the benefits were substantially outweighed. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** The parties had the opportunity to comment on the amended Framework (DL ¶3).
- **Fallback.** "I attach significant weight to that fallback position, having regard to the realistic prospect of its implementation" (DL ¶10). But the appeal scheme "would be more harmful than the fallback permission in terms of the harm to the character and appearance of the area and the living conditions of neighbouring residential occupiers" (DL ¶33).
- **Character, DP3(1): CONFLICT.** "its height, bulk and overtly boxy form would create an abrupt and jarring transition, appearing incongruous within its setback setting" (DL ¶12).
- **Living conditions: HARM (significant).** "the cumulative effect of the proposal's increased height, breadth and massing would result in an oppressive and overbearing form of development" (DL ¶17).
- **Plan weight (Annex A ¶2).** "I attribute substantial weight to the development plan policies considered as part of this submission" (DL ¶31).
- **L2(1)(d) airspace: little weight.** "However, such development should be consistent with the overall street scene. Accordingly, I attribute little weight to the proposal in this regard." (DL ¶35).
- **Flood risk.** New evidence first submitted at appeal and not scrutinised by consultees was given moderate weight and was not determinative (DL ¶24-25).

## Planning balance
Section 38(6) first, with the plan policies at substantial weight, then S4(1): "Taken together, the benefits of the proposal would be substantially outweighed by its adverse effects when assessed against the national decision-making policies of the Framework." (DL ¶37). DP3(1) is quoted in the balance but DP3(3) and S4(2)(c) are not used; the design harm is weighed as ordinary harm.

## What made the difference
The extra storey over the consented three-storey scheme. The fallback fixed the baseline, so the benefits it could equally deliver counted for little and the comparison turned on the added height. A scheme within the fallback envelope would have faced no character objection.

## Transferable points
- A fallback permission sets the baseline for both harm and benefit: benefits the fallback would also deliver attract only limited weight (DL ¶10, ¶26, ¶33).
- L2(1)(d) substantial weight for building in airspace depends on consistency with the overall street scene; where that fails the weight falls to little (DL ¶35).
- Design and amenity policies consistent with the Framework keep substantial weight under Annex A ¶2 (DL ¶31).
- Absence of harm is neutral, not a benefit (DL ¶28).
- Technical evidence first produced at appeal and untested by consultees carries reduced weight (DL ¶24-25).
PINS-6012368:
## Summary
A non-determination appeal for a small children's home in a suburban semi-detached house, allowed on the development plan. The Framework entered only through HO1, used as the yardstick for what the local plan should have evidenced about need: "it would be expected that the BLP, as required by the Framework and the LP, would provide evidence of the projected need for children’s residential care accommodation over the plan period, but it does not" (DL ¶10). The inspector found the need from the Council's own Children's Services response: "I am therefore satisfied that there is a significant ongoing need for children’s residential care accommodation in Bexley" (DL ¶10).

## What made the difference
The Council's Children's Services team confirmed that almost all referred children are placed far from the borough, which filled the gap left by the plan's silence on need. Neighbours' concerns about activity, behaviour and parking were met by a management plan, an occupancy cap of three and a two-space parking condition. No S4 balance was run because the scheme accorded with the plan.
PINS-6013634:
## Summary
A market garden in the Yorkshire Dales National Park sought a packing barn, two polytunnels and associated infrastructure. The inspector found the modest, hedge-screened buildings would have an insignificant effect on the Park's landscape, and that the existing access, although well below normal visibility standards, would not have an unacceptable impact on highway safety given the low level of movements. Policies E4 and S5 supported the horticultural use. Allowed with conditions.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** No switch paragraph. The letter cites the Framework by 2026 policy code.
- **National Park, N4(1): PASS.** "it is reasonable to expect that agricultural or horticultural uses would have buildings associated with them in order that they can function" and "the effect on the landscape value of the Park would be insignificant" (DL ¶6). The proposal would meet the N4 expectation that development be limited in scale and sensitively located and designed (DL ¶9).
- **Design, DP3: ACCORD.** The buildings "would be integrated with their surroundings in line with Policy DP3 of the Framework" (DL ¶7).
- **Highway safety, TR6(4): PASS.** "the likely low level of movements and the characteristics of the lane mean that the danger of collisions is acceptably small" (DL ¶12). "As the proposal would not have an unacceptable impact on highway safety it does not fall within the type of development that should be refused in line with the Framework." (DL ¶13).
- **Principle, S5(1)(a) and E4.** "Framework Policy S5 also establishes that development for horticulture is one of the forms of development outside settlements that should generally be approved" (DL ¶16). On securing the business benefits: "that is always likely to be the case for any commercial venture" (DL ¶17).

## Planning balance
Plan-led. No S5(1) balance was run, because no harm was found: "The proposal would conform to the development plan and there are no material considerations which indicate that a decision should not be made in accordance with it." (DL ¶22).

## What made the difference
The buildings were small, agricultural in character and sited behind a dense hedge, and the access was already in use by the business. The Authority produced no evidence of risk at the access, and the appellant's points on low speeds and light traffic went unchallenged. A new access, a larger or more exposed group of buildings, or evidence of speeds and flows on the lane could have produced a different result.

## Transferable points
- In a National Park, modest agricultural or horticultural buildings are expected features of a farmed landscape and can meet N4(1) where they are well sited (DL ¶6-9).
- A substandard visibility splay does not by itself make the impact on highway safety unacceptable under TR6(4): the existing use of the access, the likely level of movements and the character of the lane are all relevant, and the authority must evidence the risk (DL ¶10-13).
- S5(1)(a) covers horticultural development outside settlements, and E4 names polytunnels and domestic food production (DL ¶16).
- A local policy requiring removal of rural enterprise buildings when no longer needed cannot reasonably be applied to a permanent barn (DL ¶19).
- Uncertainty over whether business benefits will last is not a reason to discount them (DL ¶17).
PINS-6013769:
## Summary
A college sought to turn an occupied bookshop on St Giles' into a graduate common room, with no physical works to the Grade II listed building. The inspector found that the loss of the active shop would harm the vitality of the city centre and cause a low level of harm to the conservation area, because the retail use itself contributes to the area's significance. The moderate public benefits did not outweigh that harm under HE6(4), and under S4 the benefits were substantially outweighed. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** No switch paragraph. The letter applies the 2026 Framework by policy code (TC2, HE5, HE6, HE9, S3, S4).
- **Town centre vitality, TC2: CONFLICT.** "the proposal would reduce the range of facilities available to the wider community and … would conflict with the Framework and development plan objective of supporting the vitality of the city centre" (DL ¶10; the break is a page footnote).
- **Use as part of significance.** "the active retail use of the appeal property contributes positively to the character of this part of the city centre and, consequently, to the significance of the CA" (DL ¶11).
- **Conservation area, HE9 and HE6: HARM (low).** "the change of use of the ground floor from a commercial premises with an active ground floor frontage to a largely private, educational use would have a harmful effect on the character and significance of the CA" (DL ¶13). "Under the terms of the Framework, the proposal would result in a low level of harm to the significance of the heritage asset. It is noteworthy that even a low level of harm to the significance of a designated heritage asset carries considerable importance and weight." (DL ¶16).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "I have not been provided with substantive evidence demonstrating that alternative options have been fully explored or that the proposal represents the only reasonable solution" (DL ¶18). "the scheme’s public benefits, when considered in cumulative terms, attract moderate weight that would not outweigh the considerable importance and weight I ascribe to the harm" (DL ¶19).
- **Listed building.** No physical alterations, so the building and its setting are preserved (DL ¶2).

## Planning balance
HE6(4) was run first, on its own terms (DL ¶16-19). Then S4(1): "the benefits of granting planning permission would be substantially outweighed by adverse effects, when assessed against the Framework’s decision-making policies" (DL ¶24). The development plan conflict (V1, DH3) pointed the same way.

## What made the difference
The shop was occupied and trading, with no evidence that retail use was unviable, and it stood on a street the appraisal identifies as a historic shopping route. The college did not show why its existing common room could not be adapted or why no other space would do. Evidence of a failed retail use, or a scheme that kept an active public frontage secured as part of the description, would have changed both the vitality and the heritage findings.

## Transferable points
- A change of use with no physical works can harm a conservation area where the existing use contributes to its character and significance (DL ¶11-13, ¶15).
- The harm was found although the Council accepted the heritage effect; the inspector's own assessment governs (DL ¶13).
- Low harm to a conservation area still carries considerable importance and weight, and moderate public benefits did not outweigh it (DL ¶16, ¶19).
- Public benefits are discounted where they are not quantified and alternatives have not been explored (DL ¶18).
- Possible community use carries little weight where it is not part of the description of development (DL ¶19).
- TC2 can weigh against a proposal in a town centre: the loss of an occupied shop to a use that is not a main town centre use conflicts with the vitality objective (DL ¶9-10).
PINS-6002400:
## Summary
A communications kiosk with a digital advertising screen on Station Street, Nottingham, was dismissed (with the linked advertisement appeal). It would interrupt the long vista in which the Grade II* Midland Railway Station complex and the locally listed Trent House are appreciated, harming the conservation area and both settings. The telecommunications benefits, limited because no alternative siting had been considered, did not outweigh harm given considerable importance and weight.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties have been provided with an opportunity to comment on this matter, and I have taken account of comments made" (DL ¶3).
- **Effect.** "the kiosk would appear in lines of sight along the street, interrupting views of the listed station complex (including Forward House); and Trent House, and detracting from the long vista within the CA" (DL ¶15).
- **HE6(1)/(3): harm.** "The harm I have identified to the significance of the CA and the Grade II* listed station complex is not substantial. Nevertheless, it is of considerable importance and weight" (DL ¶22).
- **CO1 benefit, limited.** "In the absence of any compelling evidence to demonstrate any consideration of alternative sitings, I cannot be certain that the siting of the proposal is the least harmful one in heritage terms, which significantly limits the overall weight I attach to such benefits" (DL ¶26).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "Collectively, I attach moderate weight to the benefits of the proposed development, which are not sufficient to outweigh the harm I have identified to the significance of the heritage assets" (DL ¶29).
- **Advertisement appeal.** "My balancing exercise under such policies therefore only relates to the proposed development (Appeal A), and not to the proposed advertisement (Appeal B)" (DL ¶24).

## Planning balance
The HE6(4) and HE7(2) balances are run first (DL ¶21–30). S4 is then applied, but the letter puts the test the wrong way round: "the benefits would not substantially outweigh the adverse effects that I have identified. The proposed development does not therefore benefit from the presumption in favour of sustainable development" (DL ¶33). S4(1) asks whether the benefits would be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects. The heritage balance had already gone against the scheme, and the conclusion is plan-led (DL ¶34).

## What made the difference
The Grade II* station and the unbroken vista along Station Street, where existing street furniture is small and dispersed. The appellant produced no evidence of alternative sitings, which cut the CO1 weight that might otherwise have been substantial.

## Transferable points
- CO1 substantial weight for telecommunications is cut where the applicant has not shown that alternative, less harmful sitings were considered (DL ¶26).
- HE6(1) gives greater weight to conserving a Grade II* asset, and harm that is "not substantial" still carries considerable importance and weight (DL ¶21–22).
- The Framework's heritage balance applies to the planning appeal only; the advertisement appeal is decided on amenity and public safety (DL ¶4, ¶24).
- An offer to plant a street tree elsewhere, with no location or agreement, carries very little weight (DL ¶28).
- Caution: the S4 conclusion (DL ¶33) inverts the test and should not be quoted as a statement of S4(1).
PINS-6002677:
## Summary
A hybrid scheme for 352 homes on an allocated site at the southern edge of Wisbech was allowed after a hearing. The dispute was about culverting an Internal Drainage Board (IDB) watercourse to form the access. The inspector applied DM7 to assume the separate land drainage consent regime would operate effectively, found compelling reasons under F8(3) for enclosing the watercourse, and approved under S4 with substantial weight to homes that would help meet an affordable housing shortfall.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I have consulted the main parties and taken any comments into account in reaching my decision" (DL ¶3).
- **Separate regimes, DM7: PASS.** "Notwithstanding the comments of the IDB, as an application for Land Drainage Consent has not been made or determined, there is no certainty that the proposed culvert would fail to accord with the Strategy" (DL ¶13).
- **Grampian condition.** "Given the options available for the maintenance and management of the culvert, there is at least some prospect of the action being performed" (DL ¶17).
- **Culverting, F8(3): PASS.** "Any access to the site via Halfpenny Lane would require culverting at least part of the watercourse" (DL ¶22). "These matters form compelling reasons for enclosing the Halfpenny Lane watercourse such that the scheme would not conflict with the Framework in this respect" (DL ¶22).
- **Flood risk elsewhere: no harm.** "the culverting of this section of open watercourse in order to provide site access would not increase the upstream flood risk" (DL ¶20).
- **Affordable housing and viability.** 49 affordable homes; "a policy compliant scheme would be unviable" (DL ¶37).
- **S4(2): no trigger.** "While the list is not exhaustive, none of the circumstances apply in this case" (DL ¶42).

## Planning balance
S4(1), with the scheme also found to accord with the development plan (DL ¶46). Against: reduced infrastructure contributions, moderate weight, "Although there would be no associated development plan harm" (DL ¶43). For: 352 homes; the Council has a five-year supply but "a significant shortfall in affordable provision" (DL ¶44), so "I attach substantial weight to the benefit of providing affordable homes as directed by Framework Policy HO7" (DL ¶45).

## What made the difference
The allocation. It supplied both the principle and the "compelling reasons" F8(3) requires for enclosing a watercourse, since no other access was practical. The drainage board's opposition was answered by DM7 and by a negatively worded condition with some prospect of being met. Without the allocation, or with a determined refusal of land drainage consent, the F8(3) and condition findings would have been much harder.

## Transferable points
- DM7: a consenting body's statement that consent is "unlikely" is not clear evidence that a separate regime will fail, where no application has been made (DL ¶12–13).
- F8(3) "compelling reasons" for enclosing a watercourse can be an allocation combined with the absence of another suitable access (DL ¶22).
- Land allocated in a broad location for growth at a town edge was decided under S4 (DL ¶22, ¶41).
- HO7 substantial weight is available where there is a five-year supply but an evidenced affordable housing shortfall (DL ¶44–45).
- Infrastructure contributions reduced for viability can meet the Regulation 122 tests and still count as moderate harm in the S4 balance (DL ¶38, ¶43).
PINS-6002708:
## Summary
Permission in principle (PIP) for up to three homes at the northern edge of Lea was dismissed. The site is the last open buffer between modern housing and the Grade II* listed Castle End, and building on it would cause moderate harm to the asset's significance through its setting. Given considerable importance and weight, and greater weight for a Grade II* asset, that harm was not outweighed by three homes in an authority without a five-year supply.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The Council and the appellant have had opportunity to comment on this and I have taken into account any representations received" (DL ¶6).
- **Setting.** "in being mostly open from development, save for dilapidated outbuildings at the rear of the site, the appeal site does contribute positively to the setting of Castle End by being a remaining buffer" (DL ¶14).
- **HE6(1)/(3): harm, moderate.** "I find the degree of harm to the heritage asset to be at a moderate level but nevertheless is of considerable importance and weight" (DL ¶22).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "in giving considerable importance and weight to the harm to the significance of this designated heritage asset, I find that this would not be outweighed by the public benefits that the proposal would generate" (DL ¶25).
- **HE4(2): FAIL.** "the harm identified to the significance of the designated heritage asset has not been supported by clear and convincing justification" (DL ¶26).
- **Non-designated heritage assets (NDHA): not found.** "I conclude therefore on this matter that these structures do not merit NDHA status" (DL ¶20).
- **Character and appearance: no harm.** "the proposal would not harm the character and appearance of the surroundings" (DL ¶34).

## Planning balance
The heritage balance is run first (DL ¶23–26), then S5: "Framework Policy HE6 (3) sets out that any harm to a designated heritage asset will be a matter of ‘considerable importance and weight’" (DL ¶40). "I find therefore that, in accordance with Framework Policy S5, the benefits of the proposal would be substantially outweighed by the identified adverse effects" (DL ¶41). The letter does not say which S5(1) category applies. The weight given to the homes is stated two ways: moderate in ¶24 and ¶38, substantial in ¶39.

## What made the difference
The grade of the asset and the fact that this was the last undeveloped land between it and the modern estate. Limited intervisibility did not help: the open space mattered for how the listed building is experienced, and earlier development next door made the remainder more important. Nothing at PIP stage could show a layout that kept the buffer.

## Transferable points
- Setting harm does not depend on intervisibility: an open buffer can contribute to significance where views are limited by walls and planting (DL ¶10–11, ¶14).
- Development of neighbouring land increases the importance of what open setting remains (DL ¶16).
- Moderate harm to a Grade II* setting outweighs up to three homes without a five-year supply; HE6(1) gives greater weight for a more important asset (DL ¶22–25, ¶40).
- A council raising NDHA status late, on an assumption from historic maps, needs sound evidence of heritage merit (DL ¶17–20).
- At PIP stage, harm to setting from the amount and location of development is a matter of principle (DL ¶15).
PINS-6004899:
## Summary
Conversion of a farmstead in the Green Belt and the Kent Downs National Landscape to storage and light industrial units was allowed. Traffic would be similar to what the lawful agricultural use could generate, the storage and planting were contained within the farmstead, and the inspector read TR3 with E4 to accept a car-dependent location for a rural business reusing existing buildings. The scheme was not inappropriate in the Green Belt and passed the S5(5) balance with no adverse effects.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties were invited to comment on the implications of the new Framework to the appeal and the responses received have been taken into account" (DL ¶2).
- **National Landscape, N4: PASS.** "the vehicle movements associated with the proposal would not represent intensified vehicular activity or cause a reduction in the relative tranquillity of the site or this part of the landscape" (DL ¶12). "the proposal would preserve and enhance the natural beauty of the KDNL" (DL ¶16).
- **N4(2): not major.** "Given the development is largely derived from the … conversion of the existing buildings and reconfiguration of external spaces, I agree that the development should not be considered ‘major’ for the purposes of policy N4(2) of the Framework" (DL ¶15; the break is a page break).
- **Accessibility, TR3 with E4: PASS.** "Users of the appeal site are therefore very likely to be reliant on private transport rather than using more sustainable means" (DL ¶17). "It goes on to acknowledge that development proposals that meet business needs in rural areas may need to be in locations not served well by public transport" (DL ¶18). "the proposal is not one likely to generate a significant amount of movement. Neither is it apparent that the site is one where opportunities to improve walking, wheeling, cycling or public transport reasonably exist" (DL ¶19).
- **Highway safety and rights of way: PASS.** "the proposal would not increase potential harm to pedestrian safety on Fawke Wood Road" (DL ¶21).
- **Green Belt: not inappropriate.** "The development therefore complies with one of the exceptions to inappropriate development given by policy GB7 of the Framework" (DL ¶24).
- **L2: not applied.** "Since the site is not previously developed land by definition, and since the acceptability of the proposal relies on the site otherwise being used effectively for agricultural purposes, I have not applied the substantial weight set out in policy L2" (DL ¶32).

## Planning balance
S3(1)(c) and S5(5), applying S5(2). Benefits: landscape and footpath enhancements, significant biodiversity enhancements, and a district need for storage and farm diversification given significant weight; "Overall, the benefits of the scheme attract substantial weight" (DL ¶32). "the proposal would not cause any adverse effects. Accordingly, the benefits of the proposal would not be substantially outweighed by any adverse effects" (DL ¶33). No S5(2) trigger policy failed.

## What made the difference
The comparison with the lawful agricultural use: on the TRICS evidence the traffic would be similar in number and lighter in vehicle size, which answered tranquillity, highway safety and the TR3(1)(a) threshold together. E4(2) then explained why a car-dependent site was acceptable for a rural business reusing existing buildings. Evidence of materially more traffic than the farm use, or new buildings outside the farmstead, would have changed each of those findings.

## Transferable points
- TR3 is read with E4(2) for rural business proposals: a site with no footways, lighting or frequent public transport was "suitably located" for storage and light industrial reuse of farm buildings (DL ¶17–19).
- The TR3(1)(a) "significant amount of movement" judgement can be made against the movements the existing lawful use could generate (DL ¶19).
- Conversion of existing buildings and reconfigured yards is not "major" development under N4(2) (DL ¶15).
- L2 substantial weight does not apply to agricultural buildings: they are not previously developed land, and the land could otherwise be used effectively for agriculture (DL ¶32).
- A travel plan condition is not reasonable where it is unclear how the scheme could reduce car dependency (DL ¶38).
PINS-6006890:
## Summary
An outline scheme for a two-storey house in a rear garden in Harrow was dismissed on biodiversity net gain (BNG) alone. The inspector held that the newly adopted Local Plan's requirement for "comprehensive" garden-land development was materially inconsistent with L2 and gave it very limited weight, so the location was acceptable. But the de minimis exemption was not shown, no baseline was provided, and that failure substantially outweighed the benefits under S4.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "There have been significant amendments made against the 2024 version, and the parties have had the opportunity to comment on the changes in relation to this appeal" (DL ¶5).
- **BNG: FAIL.** "the de minimis exemption applies strictly to the total area of habitat impacted by the development. It does not look at the net outcome or how much habitat is intended to be restored" (DL ¶12). "I am not sufficiently satisfied that the biodiversity gain condition is capable of being successfully discharged" (DL ¶15).
- **Local policy GR10(b): CONFLICT.** "The small-scale nature of the proposals and its site size cannot reasonably be considered as making a comprehensive use of land" (DL ¶27).
- **L2(1)(d): PASS.** "The proposed development can however be reasonably considered as being broadly capable of meeting Policy L2 criteria" (DL ¶37).
- **Plan weight, Annex A ¶2.** "Parts of the criteria are different to those set out in Policy GR10 of the LP and can be reasonably described as less restrictive" (DL ¶38). "This part of the policy is therefore materially inconsistent with the Framework’s national decision-making policies" (DL ¶38). "very limited weight should be attached to criteria (b) of Policy GR10 and the associated SPD relating to garden land development" (DL ¶39).

## Planning balance
S4(1). Substantial weight to an additional home within a residential curtilage (DL ¶42). Against: "This failure constitutes a severe environmental harm which is of such overriding importance that it substantially outweighs the benefits of the scheme when assessed against the national decision-making policies in the Framework" (DL ¶43). The inspector also said that without the statutory minimum "I do not have the legal authority to grant permission" (DL ¶43). The conclusion is plan-led (DL ¶45).

## What made the difference
The absence of a habitat baseline and metric. On the same site, the same inspector allowed two bungalows the day before (PINS-6004526), where the baseline was established and the gain condition was found capable of discharge. Here the appellant's own arithmetic put the affected habitat above 25 sq m.

## Transferable points
- A local garden-land policy that adds a "comprehensive use of land" requirement is more restrictive than L2(1)(d) and gets very limited weight under Annex A ¶2, even in a plan adopted in 2026 (DL ¶6, ¶38–39). The letter does not discuss the Annex A ¶2 exception for plans examined and adopted against the new Framework.
- An SPD that interprets the inconsistent policy loses weight with it (DL ¶39).
- The BNG de minimis threshold is measured on habitat affected, not net of restoration (DL ¶12).
- A decision-maker must be satisfied the statutory gain condition can be discharged; without the Article 7 baseline information it cannot be (DL ¶14–15).
- Failure to show BNG can decide an S4 balance on its own against a substantial-weight L2 benefit (DL ¶42–43).
PINS-6008018:
## Summary
A six-bedroom guest house on the first floor of a vacant Manchester pub was dismissed. The application left out the ground floor, so the only access was through a rear yard past the bins and up a narrow stair. The inspector found the scheme was not shown to be deliverable or of the quality the local visitor-accommodation policies require, treated that as a conflict with DP3, and found the benefits substantially outweighed under S4.

## Issues and findings
- **Plan weight, Annex A ¶2.** "Policy CC4 of the CS and policy 4.1 of the UDP are not materially inconsistent with the national decision making policies within the Framework" (DL ¶11), "as they are policies which seek to assist in creating well designed places, which is a key principle of Framework Policy DP3" (DL ¶11).
- **Principle: CONFLICT.** "I cannot be assured that the accommodation as a whole would be of an appropriate quality or offer good ease of access for all" (DL ¶16).
- **Living conditions and parking: acceptable.** "There is nothing compelling to indicate that any, likely limited, increased parking demand in association with this proposal would cause any unacceptable additional parking stress or cause harm to highway safety" (DL ¶25).
- **DP3 and S4: FAIL.** "There would be conflict with Policy DP3 and the benefits of approving the scheme would be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶31).

## Planning balance
S4(1). For: reuse of a vacant building, some employment, support for tourism (DL ¶28).
