Against: "serious doubts over the design quality of the scheme before me" because access for all is not assured (DL ¶29). The DP3 conflict is derived from "development plan policy relating to the design standards for this type of accommodation with regard to access" (DL ¶31). DP3(3) is not cited and no clear-justification question is asked.

## What made the difference
The red line and description. By excluding the ground floor, through which the first floor must be reached, the scheme could not show a workable or good-quality access. An application covering both floors with a proper entrance would have met the main objection.

## Transferable points
- Local policies on the quality of visitor accommodation were held not materially inconsistent with the Framework, by reference to DP3, and kept full weight (DL ¶11).
- A conflict with a local standard on access quality was treated as a DP3 conflict and weighed in the S4 balance (DL ¶31).
- A scheme whose access depends on land or floorspace outside the application is not shown to be deliverable (DL ¶14, ¶29).
PINS-6008122:
## Summary
A replacement house in the Green Belt at Canewdon was dismissed on biodiversity net gain (BNG) alone. The inspector found the scheme not inappropriate under GB7(1)(e) and cut the conflicting local replacement-dwelling policy to very limited weight. But the self-build exemption from BNG could not lawfully be secured by the occupancy condition both parties had agreed, and with no baseline evidence the statutory requirement was not met. That harm substantially outweighed the limited benefits in the S5(5) balance.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I have considered the comments made by the main parties on this matter" (DL ¶4).
- **Self-build condition, DM6: FAIL.** "compliance with it would depend on the continued occupation of the dwelling by a particular person. If for any reason that person ceased to occupy the dwelling before the end of the specified period, the self-build exemption would no longer apply" (DL ¶8). "the suggested condition would be in conflict with the PPG and would therefore fail the tests of reasonableness and enforceability set out in Framework policy DM6" (DL ¶9).
- **BNG: FAIL.** "In the absence of evidence of the site's pre-development biodiversity value, there is no basis upon which compliance with the statutory BNG requirements could be determined" (DL ¶10).
- **GB7(1)(e): PASS.** "Whilst the proposal would replace an existing dwelling, it would also redevelop PDL" (DL ¶15). Neither the evidence nor the case law suggested "that a proposal falling within one category of Policy GB7 cannot also be considered against another" (DL ¶15). "Any resulting harm to openness would therefore fall short of the high threshold of substantial harm" (DL ¶16).
- **Plan weight, Annex A ¶2.** "Policy DM21 of the DMP does not contemplate that exception. It is therefore materially inconsistent with Framework policy GB7 as it applies to this proposal" (DL ¶17).
- **N2(1)(a): CONFLICT.** "there would be conflict with Framework policy N2(1)(a), to which I attach significant weight" (DL ¶23).

## Planning balance
S5(5): "As the site lies outside a settlement, Framework policy S5(5) is engaged" (DL ¶21). Benefits each limited: an open-market replacement dwelling with no evidence of need, private design preferences, and short-term construction activity (DL ¶22). Against: the N2(1)(a) conflict, significant weight. "The benefits of the proposal would be substantially outweighed by its adverse effects when assessed against the Framework's national decision-making policies" (DL ¶23). The appeal failed on material considerations despite no conflict with the plan as a whole (DL ¶24).

## What made the difference
The absence of a baseline biodiversity assessment, combined with reliance on a self-build exemption that could only be secured by a personal occupancy condition. A planning obligation securing self-build, or a metric showing how 10% would be delivered, would have left nothing against the scheme.

## Transferable points
- A condition tying occupation to the person who commissioned the house, for a fixed period, fails the DM6 tests: permission runs with the land, and the biodiversity effects outlast any change of occupier (DL ¶8–9).
- Agreement between council and appellant that self-build can be secured by condition does not bind the inspector (DL ¶7–9).
- A replacement dwelling that may fail GB7(1)(b) can be tested under GB7(1)(e) as redevelopment of PDL; the categories are alternatives (DL ¶15).
- A local replacement-dwelling policy limiting bulk and massing is materially inconsistent with GB7(1)(e) and gets very limited weight under Annex A ¶2 (DL ¶17).
- Not-inappropriate Green Belt development with no plan conflict can still be refused in the S5(5) balance on an unmet statutory BNG requirement (DL ¶21–24).
- HO7 weight for a one-for-one replacement dwelling is limited (DL ¶22).
PINS-6008177:
## Summary
Permission in principle for 5 to 9 dwellings on a field beside the B6047 at Market Harborough was allowed. The inspector found that the visibility splays the highway authority required depend on third-party land and could not be secured with certainty, and that the conservation officer saw potential harm to the adjoining canal conservation area and to ridge and furrow on the site. Both matters were nonetheless left to the technical details stage: the splay constraint might be overcome, and with only a red-line plan there was no demonstrated heritage harm. The letter applies neither S4 nor S5 and runs no planning balance.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** No switch paragraph. The Framework is cited only for HE9 and HE7 (DL ¶27-28).
- **Scope of permission in principle.** "It is not inappropriate for the Council to have considered these matters, which are fundamental to whether a development would be acceptable in principle" (DL ¶4).
- **Highway safety: splays not secured.** "Whilst the provision and maintenance of visibility splays can be secured by planning condition, it would be difficult to enforce and ensure compliance where the required land lies within third-party ownership." (DL ¶18). "there is no certainty that the splays could be provided in the first instance or maintained for the lifetime of the development" and "this would give rise to an unacceptable risk to highway safety for users of the B6047 without the provision of adequate visibility splays" (DL ¶19).
- **Highway safety: deferred, location acceptable.** "these constraints do not appear to me to be so severe that there would be no possibility at all for this to be overcome as part of the future detailed site design at the technical details consent stage" and "The land which is owned by a third party could be acquired, or a detailed management agreement be provided prior to the submission of a technical details consent application in the future." (DL ¶21).
- **Pedestrian access: deferred.** "this location is absent of meaningful and dedicated pedestrian infrastructure" (DL ¶22).
- **Heritage: potential harm, not assessed.** "there is potential for harm to both the CA and the NDHA through the loss of historic features" but "given the limited information submitted in support of a permission in principle application, it is difficult to undertake a detailed assessment of the extent of any such harm" (DL ¶29).
- **Heritage: no demonstrated harm.** "On the evidence before me, I therefore find no demonstrated harm to either heritage asset at this stage." (DL ¶31). "Critically, there is no evidence at this stage to demonstrate the proposal would not meet these requirements." (DL ¶35).

## Planning balance
None. The inspector found no conflict with local plan policies GD8, IN2 and HC1 at this stage (DL ¶23, ¶35) and allowed the appeal "taking all material considerations into account" (DL ¶38). There is no S4 or S5 analysis, no weighing of housing benefits and no HE6(4) or HE7(2) balance, because no harm was found.

## What made the difference
The inspector's view of what the first stage decides. Each unresolved matter (third-party splay land, the lack of a footway, and the effect of up to nine houses on the canal's setting and on the ridge and furrow) was treated as capable of resolution at technical details stage, and the absence of evidence of harm was treated as no harm. Other appeal decisions in this database treat a splay over third-party land as fatal and not curable by condition (PINS-6006496 ¶22-23; PINS-6009997 ¶14-15).

## Transferable points
- This letter is an outlier and should be cited with care: it defers to the technical details stage a splay that depends on third-party land, after finding the risk unacceptable without it (DL ¶19, ¶21).
- The test applied to an in-principle highway constraint was whether there is "no possibility at all" of overcoming it (DL ¶21).
- An evidence gap on heritage at permission in principle stage was resolved in the appellant's favour: "no demonstrated harm" (DL ¶31), where the conservation officer had identified potential harm (DL ¶29).
- Highways and heritage are proper matters for a council to consider at permission in principle stage (DL ¶4, ¶32).
- Recorded collisions near a proposed access were attributed to driver judgement, not to an unsafe arrangement (DL ¶14).
- The closing sentence on heritage is garbled: the proposal "would not harm the setting of the CA, or would fail to conserve the NDHA" (DL ¶35).
PINS-6009135:
## Summary
A two-storey side extension and conversion to create two more flats at the end of a small parade in Wednesfield was dismissed. The extension would dominate an open corner and breach the building line, and the shared amenity space and the relationship with one ground-floor flat were poor. The inspector tied both harms to the L2(1)(d) criteria and found the benefits substantially outweighed under S4.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "the provisions in respect of the matters relied on by the main parties are not materially changed. Therefore, I did not need to consult with the main parties regarding the revised Framework" (DL ¶2).
- **Character: harm.** "the proposal would demonstrably harm the appearance of the streetscene" (DL ¶9).
- **Living conditions: harm.** The scheme would "create a poor relationship for the occupiers of flat 3 with users of the external space, resulting in poor living conditions through inadequate privacy, and unacceptable levels of noise and general disturbance" (DL ¶18).
- **Parking and highway safety: acceptable.** "the proposal would not create a significant increase in on-street parking pressure or result in an adverse effect on highway safety" (DL ¶24).
- **L2(1)(d)(i) and (ii): CONFLICT.** "the proposal would not be consistent with the overall streetscene, in conflict with policy L2(1)(d)(i) of the Framework. The scheme would also create poor living standards for existing and future residents, in terms of provision of external space and effect on privacy, as sought by the Framework’s policy L2(1)(d)(ii)" (DL ¶32).

## Planning balance
S4(1), after a plan-led finding of conflict given significant weight (DL ¶29). HO7 and the accessible location weigh in favour (DL ¶30–31). "the benefits of the proposed development, would be substantially outweighed by the identified adverse effects of the proposal, when assessed against the national decision-making policies of the Framework as a whole" (DL ¶33). DP3 is not cited; the design harm is routed through L2(1)(d)(i).

## What made the difference
The corner. The existing single-storey extension left space above it, and a full-height addition close to the footway would end that openness. A scheme confined to the change of use, or with a set-back upper floor and a usable private amenity area, would have avoided both harms.

## Transferable points
- The L2(1)(d) criteria work as tests of harm as well as conditions for L2 weight: street-scene inconsistency and poor external space or privacy were recorded as conflicts with L2(1)(d)(i) and (ii) (DL ¶32).
- Nearby public open space does not make up for poor on-site amenity space for flats (DL ¶15).
- Meeting a maximum parking standard and showing fewer trips than the lawful commercial use answered the parking objection (DL ¶19–20, ¶24).
PINS-6009363:
## Summary
Outline permission for nine houses on a 1.3 ha field next to Brigsley's development boundary was dismissed. With no five-year supply, the site met S5(1)(j) as physically well-related to the settlement, and nine homes had substantial weight. But at 6.8 dwellings per hectare the scheme did not make effective use of land, and L3(4) says such proposals should be refused. That engaged S5(2). With a poorly connected location and landscape harm each given considerable weight, the benefits were substantially outweighed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties have had the opportunity to comment on the content of the National Planning Policy Framework 2026 (Framework) including Policy L3; and given its expectations, the effective use of land has been included within the main issues." (DL ¶3).
- **Plan weight (Annex A ¶2): part by part.** Of Local Plan Policy 5 Part 1: "This is generally consistent with the Framework and can be afforded full weight. Part 3 of the policy is inconsistent with the Framework and can be afforded very limited weight." (DL ¶4).
- **S5(1)(j)(i): PASS.** "As it is accepted that the local planning authority cannot demonstrate a five year supply of deliverable housing sites, it … satisfies Policy S5(1ji) in that it would be physically well-related to an existing settlement." (DL ¶5; the break is a page break).
- **Density, L3: FAIL.** "I am not persuaded that the provision of nine dwellings on this site represents an effective use of land or satisfies Framework Policy L3. In these circumstances, the policy is clear that the development should be refused." (DL ¶9).
- **DP3(3): NOT TRIGGERED.** "the details of design are reserved matters and it would not result in clear conflict with Policy DP3 to the extent that it would trigger the requirement that it should be refused" (DL ¶12). The landscape harm is instead recorded against N2(1)(a) (DL ¶11).
- **Location, TR3(1)(a): FAIL.** "The Framework defines a reasonable walking distance as being around 800m. Distances from the site are prohibitive for walking to schools, shops and healthcare facilities." and "as no evidence is provided with regard to bus frequency, it cannot be assumed that a convenient service would be available" (DL ¶14). "The site performs poorly with regard to the promotion of sustainable travel and it does not offer a genuine choice of transport modes for residents." (DL ¶17).
- **Housing, HO7: substantial.** "The provision of houses must be given substantial weight." (DL ¶21).

## Planning balance
S5(1) with S5(2): "These conflicts, particularly but not limited to Framework Policy L3, represent the circumstances, set out in Framework Policy S5(2), in which the benefits of approving development proposals are likely to be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects." (DL ¶24). Substantial weight to nine homes and considerable weight to social and economic benefits, with biodiversity and tree planting in support, against the L3 refusal policy and considerable weight each to the TR3 conflict and the landscape harm.

## What made the difference
Density. The site passed the S5(1)(j) gateway and the housing benefit had full weight, but nine houses on 1.3 ha could not be called the best use of the site's potential, and the appellant gave no net density figure. The inspector raised L3 after the Framework changed. A denser scheme would have removed the refusal policy, though it would have sharpened the landscape and location objections, which also carried considerable weight.

## Transferable points
- L3(2)(b) and L3(4) apply to housing on unallocated land outside a settlement that relies on S5(1)(j); very low density is a "should be refused" failure that engages S5(2) (DL ¶7-9, ¶24).
- An inspector may add effective use of land as a main issue after consulting the parties on the new Framework (DL ¶3).
- Local support for low density and the character of neighbouring housing did not justify a very low density (DL ¶9).
- At outline stage with design reserved, harm to the character of the area was held not to be a clear DP3 conflict triggering DP3(3); it was weighed under N2(1)(a) instead (DL ¶11-12).
- A site adjoining the development boundary was treated as physically well-related to the settlement without further analysis (DL ¶5, ¶22).
- Bus stops without evidence of frequency do not show a convenient service (DL ¶14).
- The Annex B "around 800m" reasonable walking distance was used as the measure for walking to services, beyond the station policies it is written for (DL ¶14).
- A local plan policy can be split under Annex A ¶2, one part at full weight and another at very limited weight (DL ¶4).
PINS-6009720:
## Summary
Permission in principle (PIP) for one dwelling in the Green Belt on the edge of Hitchin was allowed. The inspector found the site to be grey belt, although it adjoins a large built-up area and sits in a parcel the Council's review rates as strong, because containment made its own contribution moderate. GB7(1)(g) was met and the S5(5) balance favoured approval.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties were given an opportunity to comment on the implications of the revised Framework for the appeal" (DL ¶5).
- **Purpose (a): moderate.** Because of the site's partial enclosure, "the proposed development would not result in an incongruous pattern of development. These features would also serve to restrict and contain the proposed development to an extent" (DL ¶12).
- **Purpose (b): moderate.** "Due to its small size and the existing intervening features between the towns, including roads and vegetation, the site could be developed without resulting in the loss of visual separation between the towns" (DL ¶13).
- **Grey belt: PASS.** "the site does not strongly contribute to the relevant purposes of the Green Belt and therefore comprises grey belt land" (DL ¶15).
- **GB7(1)(g)(iii) / TR3: PASS.** "There are bus stops and footpaths in close proximity to the site which would be available for use by future occupants to access Hitchin town centre. Due to its proximity to, and access to, different modes of transport, the site would be in a sustainable location" (DL ¶19). On the missing frontage footway: "Even if it was considered as part of this first stage, due to the scale of the development, it would not result in a significant adverse impact on the transport network" (DL ¶20).
- **S5(5), not S5(1)(j).** "the decision is to be made by applying the approach set out in part (5) of Policy S5 rather than part (1)(j)" (DL ¶28).
- **Openness.** "there is no need to consider its impact on the openness of the Green Belt" (DL ¶22).

## Planning balance
S5(5). Substantial weight to one dwelling under HO7 and limited weight to economic benefits (DL ¶30). Limited weight to the conflict with Local Plan SP2 (DL ¶29). "I have not identified any adverse effects that would substantially outweigh the benefits" (DL ¶31).

## What made the difference
Containment: housing to the west, an elevated railway to the south and vegetation to the east meant the site itself made only a moderate contribution to purpose (a), whatever the rating of the wider parcel. The location limb was passed on a general statement of nearby bus stops and footpaths, with the missing frontage footway deferred to the technical details stage. Evidence that the walk involved the carriageway might have produced a different answer on limb (iii).

## Transferable points
- Land adjoining a town can still be grey belt: containment features of the kind listed in Annex E reduce the contribution to purpose (a) to moderate (DL ¶11–12).
- The site is assessed, not the review parcel: a parcel rated strong for purposes (a) and (b) did not prevent a moderate finding for a small enclosed plot (DL ¶10–13).
- Where a council argues S5(1)(j) on a Green Belt site, S5(5) is the correct route (DL ¶28).
- Once GB7(1)(g) is met, openness is not assessed (DL ¶22).
- Caution: limb (iii) was passed without distances, frequencies or a route assessment (DL ¶19–20), so the letter is weak authority on the sustainable-location test.
PINS-6009880:
## Summary
An appeal to extend the hours during which cafe furniture and barriers may stand on Scarborough's East Pier was dismissed. Leaving them out until 22:00 through the tourist season would erode the open harbourside setting of the listed pier and the character of the conservation area, at the lower end of the scale. The modest benefit of extra trading hours did not outweigh that harm, so the condition was necessary and reasonable.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "In the interests of procedural fairness, the parties were given an opportunity to comment on the implications for the appeal" (DL ¶2).
- **Harm: lower end.** The effects would be seasonal and limited in extent: "The resulting heritage harm would therefore be at the lower end of the scale" (DL ¶11).
- **Benefits: modest.** "The benefits before me are therefore confined to those arising from the additional period during which the furniture and barriers could remain in place. In that context, the public benefits would be modest" (DL ¶12).
- **Weight.** "The Framework makes clear that harm to the significance of a heritage asset is a matter of considerable importance and that substantial weight should be given to the asset’s conservation" (DL ¶13).
- **Balance: FAIL.** "the modest public benefits arising from the additional period during which the furniture and barriers could remain in place would not outweigh the identified heritage harm" (DL ¶14).

## Planning balance
The heritage balance only, in Framework terms but without policy numbers. Harm to the non-designated Toll Bar is added to the designated-asset harm: "the collective heritage harm carries substantial weight in the balance" (DL ¶13).

## What made the difference
The baseline. The seating area already had permission, so the only benefit was the extra hours, while the harm came from furniture standing in an otherwise open historic harbour setting for much longer each day.

## Transferable points
- On an appeal against a condition, the public benefits are those of the variation sought, not of the development already permitted (DL ¶12).
- Seasonal and temporary paraphernalia can harm the setting of a listed structure where openness contributes to its significance (DL ¶7, ¶10–11).
- Lower-end harm to a listed building's setting and a conservation area outweighs modest commercial benefits (DL ¶13–14).
PINS-6009910:
## Summary
A two-storey house and double garage in the rear garden of a semi-detached house on a corner plot in Whetstone was dismissed. It would break the pattern of houses fronting the street with long rear gardens, and the fixed obscure glazing needed to protect neighbours would leave future occupiers with a poor outlook and very small gardens. Under S4 the limited benefit of one home, without a five-year supply, was substantially outweighed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I have not sought the views of the main parties on the revised Framework as the policies relating to the main issues of this appeal have not significantly changed" (DL ¶3).
- **Character: significant harm.** "A two-storey dwelling together with a double garage would fill a significant proportion of the rear garden of No.12 with development, harming the existing sense of space around dwellings" (DL ¶6).
- **Living conditions: harm.** "Only having clear glazing and opening first floor windows on the front elevation with no outlook to the sides or rear of the property would provide a sub-standard experience for occupiers of the property" (DL ¶10).
- **S4(1): FAIL.** "The addition of one dwelling would be limited in this context and is therefore substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶14).

## Planning balance
S4(1) in two paragraphs. The harms are found against local plan policies only; no Framework design or amenity policy is named, and the DP3(3) question is not asked (DL ¶8, ¶12–14).

## What made the difference
The site was too tight: protecting the neighbours required glazing that made the house itself unsatisfactory. A single-storey building, in keeping with the outbuildings found in neighbouring gardens, would not have raised the same issues.

## Transferable points
- Local-plan-only harms to character and living conditions can substantially outweigh one home under S4(1), even without a five-year supply (DL ¶13–14).
- Obscure, fixed glazing that solves overlooking can create a separate harm to future occupiers (DL ¶9–10).
PINS-6009979:
## Summary
An appeal against a condition preventing uPVC frames in a ground-floor shopfront in the Barnoldswick Conservation Area was dismissed. uPVC would not replicate the slender timber shopfront that contributes to the area's commercial character, causing harm at the lower end of the spectrum. The benefits claimed did not depend on using uPVC, so they did not outweigh the harm under HE6, and the condition was reasonable and necessary.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties were provided with an opportunity to comment. I have had regard to the 2026 version of the Framework in my decision" (DL ¶3).
- **Harm: lower end, HE6(3).** "Based on the information before me, the magnitude of this harm would be towards the lower end of the spectrum. Nevertheless, having regard to my statutory duty, I attach considerable importance and weight to that harm" (DL ¶9).
- **HE4(2) and HE6(4) stated.** "Policy HE4 of the Framework sets out that any harm to, or loss of, the significance of a designated heritage asset should have a clear and convincing justification. Policy HE6 goes on to state that the effect on the asset and its significance should be weighed against any public benefits resulting from the proposal" (DL ¶10).
- **Benefits not dependent on the harm.** "these improvements would not be dependent on the use of uPVC for the ground-floor shopfront and could equally be achieved through the use of a more appropriate alternative material" (DL ¶11).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "the public benefits of the use of uPVC for the shopfront would not outweigh the considerable importance and weight that should be attached to the identified harm to the CA and the substantial weight that should be given to its conservation, irrespective of the level of harm" (DL ¶13).

## Planning balance
HE6(4) only: lower-end harm, given considerable importance and weight, against benefits each given limited weight (DL ¶11–13). No S4 balance.

## What made the difference
The benefits (removing plastic cladding upstairs, reusing a door, supporting the business) could all be had with timber at street level. Evidence that timber was not viable, which was asserted but not produced, might have added weight but would not have removed the harm.

## Transferable points
- HE6(1) and HE6(3) stated together and correctly: considerable importance and weight to the harm, substantial weight to conservation "irrespective of the level of harm" (DL ¶13).
- Public benefits that do not depend on the harmful element, and could be achieved with a more appropriate material, carry limited weight in the HE6(4) balance (DL ¶11–12).
- Other unauthorised or immune uPVC in a conservation area does not justify more (DL ¶16).
- An unevidenced claim that the cost of an alternative material would jeopardise a business does not outweigh heritage harm (DL ¶17).
PINS-6010033:
## Summary
A takeaway and delivery-only food use in a former barber shop in Hackney was dismissed. The premises are about 315 m from a school and outside any designated centre, contrary to the local 400 m exclusion policy and to Framework policy HC5. Activity from delivery riders and walk-in customers on a narrow pavement beside a Red Route would also have an unacceptable impact on highway safety under TR6(4).

## Issues and findings
- **HC5: CONFLICT.** "if permission were to be granted for a sui generis use it would not be possible to control by condition or any other means the proportion of walk-in orders, including from children, compared with deliveries" (DL ¶6). The scheme would be "in harmful conflict with Local Plan Policy LP39; London Plan Policy E9 and with Government policy in Policy HC5 of the recently revised National Planning Policy Framework August 2026" (DL ¶7).
- **TR6(4): FAIL.** "the comings and goings from cycles, motorbikes and cars associated with premises on a site with a narrow pavement, very limited parking and fronting onto a Red Route highway would be such as to result in an increase in hazards and overall have an unacceptable impact on highway safety" (DL ¶11).

## Planning balance
None is run. Each issue is a conflict with the plan and with a Framework policy that says development should be refused, and "the appeal fails" (DL ¶12). S4 is not mentioned.

## What made the difference
The use class. Permission would be for a sui generis takeaway, and no condition could hold the operator to deliveries only or to a particular menu. The delivery-led business model therefore did not answer either the school-proximity policy or the Red Route parking problem.

## Transferable points
- HC5 is applied alongside a local 400 m school exclusion zone; a site about 315 m from a school and outside a designated centre conflicts with both (DL ¶3–4, ¶7).
- A delivery-only or healthier-food business model carries little weight where the permission could not control walk-in sales or the food sold (DL ¶6).
- TR6(4) "unacceptable impact on highway safety" can arise from delivery and customer activity at premises with no lawful stopping place (DL ¶8–11).
PINS-6010376:
## Summary
Conversion and upward extension of a former school building in Hull to 37 student bedrooms was dismissed on design alone. The inspector found against the Council on the loss of a community use, the concentration of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) and neighbours' privacy. But the extensions conflicted with DP3(1) without clear justification, which engaged the S4(2)(c) refusal trigger and outweighed the benefits.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "Both main parties have been given the opportunity to comment on how the changes affect their respective cases" (DL ¶3).
- **Character, DP3(1): CONFLICT.** The extension would create "an illegible form of development that would appear as a top-heavy addition … to the building" (DL ¶9; the break is a page break). Low prominence "is not a reason to justify the poor design quality of the proposed development" (DL ¶11).
- **Community use, HC6: held not engaged.** "There is no mention of schools within Policy HC6 or within the definition of community facilities, consequently the existing use at the appeal site would not be regarded as a community use for the purpose of the Framework" (DL ¶28). The letter does not refer to the separate Annex B definition of "public service infrastructure", which HC6 also protects.
- **Plan weight, Annex A ¶2.** Development plan policies "which are materially inconsistent with national decision-making policies in the Framework, such as HLP Policy 13 in this case regarding a school as a community use, should be given very limited weight" (DL ¶28).
- **HMO concentration: no conflict.** "there is no evidence before me that the proposed development would breach the 50% threshold along the entire street" (DL ¶42).
- **Housing weight, HO7.** "I attach only modest weight to its provision, and not the substantial weight as advocated within Policy HO7" (DL ¶68).
- **L2 airspace.** The character harm "significantly limits the weight afforded to that part of the policy in this case" (DL ¶67).
- **DP3(3): FAIL.** "where there is conflict with this part of the policy, without clear justification (as in this case) the development should be refused" (DL ¶69).

## Planning balance
Plan-led, with S4 as a material consideration. S4(2)(c) is paraphrased: "where there is conflict with one of the national decision-making policies which state that development proposals should be refused, this is likely to indicate the benefits are substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶70). Benefits: modest weight to the accommodation, substantial-weight policies CC2, CC3 and L2 acknowledged but discounted because a better designed reuse could deliver them or because of the character harm (DL ¶66–68). The benefits "are not considered to outweigh the conflict with Policy DP3" (DL ¶70).

## What made the difference
The design of the extensions. Every other issue went the appellant's way, including a plan-policy conflict on loss of a community use that the inspector set aside under Annex A ¶2. A scheme that reused the building with extensions respecting its symmetry and the adjoining church would probably have succeeded on this reasoning.

## Transferable points
- A DP3(1) conflict without clear justification engages S4(2)(c), and outweighs CC2, CC3 and L2 substantial-weight benefits that a better designed scheme could also deliver (DL ¶66, ¶69–70).
- HO7 substantial weight depends on an evidenced need: student accommodation with no demonstrated need, and which the University said was not required, got modest weight despite a 3.16-year supply (DL ¶60, ¶68).
- L2(1)(d) support for airspace development is conditional on street-scene and character tests; harm there "significantly limits" the weight (DL ¶67).
- A whole-street HMO threshold must be measured over the whole street; council sub-area calculations did not show a breach (DL ¶41–42).
- Caution: the letter's reading that schools fall outside HC6 (DL ¶28) does not deal with the Annex B definition of "public service infrastructure", which includes education facilities. It should not be cited for that point without checking the definition.
PINS-6010445:
## Summary
A communications hub with a digital advertising screen on the Fulham Road footway, inside the Walham Green Conservation Area, was dismissed with its linked advertisement appeal. The harm to the conservation area was at the lower level, but the benefits, although given substantial weight in principle, were modest in scale and did not outweigh it under HE6(4). The scheme also failed on highway safety: driver distraction at a busy junction and obstruction of pedestrians at a pinch point.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties have been consulted and provided with an opportunity to provide … comments on it in relation to these appeals" (DL ¶4; the break is a page break).
- **Character: harm.** "it would have an undue presence in its setting, appearing as an incongruous and uncharacteristic feature" (DL ¶10).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "Whilst the degree of harm resulting from the proposed Hub and advertisement on the significance of the Walham Green CA would be at the lower level, in accordance with Policy HE6 (4) of the Framework, that harm should be weighed against any public benefits of the proposals" (DL ¶14). "whilst afforded substantial weight in line with the policies in the Framework, given the limited scale of the proposals, these benefits would be modest. I therefore find insufficient public benefits arising from the proposals to offset the identified harm to which I attach substantial weight" (DL ¶16).
- **Highway safety: harm.** "the proposals would result in increased potential risk of collision between motorists and/or pedestrians/cyclists and as such would have an unacceptable effect on highways safety" (DL ¶20).
- **Off-site kiosk removal.** "I am not satisfied this would mitigate the harm arising from the appeal proposals, nor that a planning condition to secure its removal would meet the tests on conditions set out in the Framework" (DL ¶26).

## Planning balance
HE6(4): lower-level harm to a conservation area against benefits that carry substantial weight in principle but are modest in scale. No S4 balance is run; the conclusion is plan-led (DL ¶30).

## What made the difference
The junction. A lit screen close to the kerb at a multi-lane roundabout with a collision record, on a corner where the footway narrows, failed on safety whatever the heritage balance. The absence of other illuminated advertisements in the footway made the hub more prominent on both issues.

## Transferable points
- Substantial weight in principle for communications infrastructure does not make the benefits large: a single hub's benefits were "modest" and lost the HE6(4) balance to lower-level harm (DL ¶16).
- Removing a kiosk at another site in the borough does not mitigate harm at the appeal site and cannot be secured by condition (DL ¶26).
- A measured clear footway width does not answer obstruction where the footway narrows at a corner and pedestrians were seen to cross the proposed position (DL ¶22–23).
PINS-6010951:
## Summary
One self-build house at Clavering was dismissed although the inspector found the site to be within the village and in a sustainable location, so that S4 applied. The access crossed Flood Zones 2 and 3 with no sequential test and no demonstrated safe escape route, and the self-build unilateral undertaking (UU) was too defective to secure the biodiversity net gain (BNG) exemption. Those harms substantially outweighed the benefit of one home.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The parties were given an opportunity to comment on the implications of the revised Framework for the appeal" (DL ¶4).
- **Sequential test, F5: FAIL.** "Part 2(b)(i) is not met as built development within the site boundary, including access or escape routes, would be located in an area that would be at risk of flooding from any source, now and in the future" (DL ¶13). "no sequential test has been undertaken, and I have not been provided with sufficient evidence to demonstrate that there are no reasonably available sites at a lower risk of flooding" (DL ¶15).
- **Safety, F7: FAIL.** The flood risk assessment "does not demonstrate how the site could be safely accessed or provide definitive escape routes in a flooding event" (DL ¶12).
- **Self-build and BNG: FAIL.** "On the basis of what is before me I am not satisfied that the development can be considered to be custom or self-build and the proposal has also failed to demonstrate that it would make appropriate provision for BNG" (DL ¶18).
- **Location: within the settlement, S4.** "the site is perceived as forming part of the built area within the village. It does not perform the role of a distinct gap within the settlement" (DL ¶23).
- **Accessibility: PASS.** "Whilst the roads are unlit, the presence of footways and the 30 miles per hour speed limit assists in making the routes reasonably accessible for pedestrians and cyclists" (DL ¶25).

## Planning balance
S4(1). Against: flood risk, substantial weight (DL ¶28); failure to meet the statutory BNG provisions, significant weight (DL ¶29). For: one dwelling at 4.77 years, substantial weight (DL ¶30); biodiversity enhancements and economic benefits, moderate weight together (DL ¶31). Self-build carried no weight as it was unsecured (DL ¶19, ¶29). "the adverse effects and policy conflicts identified in relation to flood risk and BNG are considerable and weigh heavily against the proposal, such that they substantially outweigh the benefits of the proposal" (DL ¶32).

## What made the difference
The access, not the house, was in the flood zone, and that alone took the scheme outside the F5(2)(b)(i) exemption. With a sequential test, evidence of a dry or safe escape route, and a properly executed self-build undertaking, the inspector's findings on location and S4 would have supported approval.

## Transferable points
- An access or escape route in Flood Zones 2 or 3 engages the sequential test under F5(2)(b)(i), even where the dwelling is in Flood Zone 1 (DL ¶13).
- An inspector may raise the sequential test where the council did not, after inviting comments (DL ¶2, ¶8).
- Failure of the sequential test is weighed in the S4 balance rather than treated as automatically fatal, and still attracted substantial weight (DL ¶14, ¶28).
- A self-build UU with no title evidence, no plan and no occupancy period secures neither the BNG exemption nor any self-build benefit (DL ¶18–19).
- Where a village has no defined boundary, whether a site is within the built area is a planning judgement on containment and the pattern of development (DL ¶21–23).
PINS-6011062:
## Summary
A three-storey extra-care extension (13 net Class C2 units) at a riverside retirement village in the Green Belt opposite Henley was dismissed. The heritage harm to two conservation areas was limited and was outweighed by substantial public benefits under HE6(4). The appeal failed on living conditions: the overbearing effect and overlooking of 1 to 5 Remenham Row conflicted with DP3, there was no clear justification, and S5(2) then indicated refusal.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "Comments were sought from the main parties on the implications of the revised Framework for the determination of the appeal" (DL ¶2).
- **Living conditions, DP3(1): CONFLICT.** "the proposal would result in both an overbearing relationship and a harmful loss of privacy for the existing occupants of Remenham Row" (DL ¶17). It would "conflict with Policy DP3 of the Framework, which requires development to respond positively to its context so that it integrates with and enhances its surroundings" (DL ¶17).
- **P3: not determinative.** "that policy is principally concerned with living conditions in relation to matters such as daylight and sunlight, together with air, noise, light, water and other forms of pollution" (DL ¶18).
- **Heritage, HE6(1)/(3)/(4): harm limited, OUTWEIGHED.** "I find that the degree of harm would be limited. Nevertheless, Policy HE6.1 of the Framework states that substantial weight should be given to the conservation of designated heritage assets. I have therefore attached considerable importance and weight to that harm" (DL ¶30). "Having attached considerable importance and weight to the identified heritage harm, I nevertheless find that these substantial public benefits outweigh that harm" (DL ¶37).
- **Green Belt: not inappropriate.** "I am satisfied that the proposal would constitute not inappropriate development in the Green Belt, comprising the partial redevelopment of previously developed land" (DL ¶39).
- **DP3(3): FAIL.** "While the benefits I outline above are significant, they do not in my view, provide clear justification to allow development that would harm the living conditions of the existing residents in the manner I have described" (DL ¶44).
- **S5(2): FAIL.** "As I have found that the proposal conflicts with Policy DP3, I consider this to be such a case. Accordingly, I find that the benefits of the proposal would be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶45).

## Planning balance
Two balances were run. The HE6(4) heritage balance came first and was passed: significant weight to 13 net units, significant weight to older persons' need, and moderate weight to land use, environmental, and economic and social benefits, against limited harm given considerable importance and weight (DL ¶30–37). The principle was then tested under S5(1)(d) and S5(2), not S5(5), although the site is in the Green Belt (DL ¶39, ¶41). The DP3(3) failure decided it (DL ¶43–45), and the conclusion is plan-led (DL ¶47).

## What made the difference
The neighbours' frontage was private, on lower ground, and faced by new upper-floor living-room windows, so compliance with separation guidelines did not answer the harm. Benefits large enough to outweigh conservation-area harm were still not a "clear justification" for amenity harm to five homes. A lower building at the northern end, without the third floor, would have addressed both the neighbours and Historic England's concern.

## Transferable points
- DP3(1) and DP3(3) were applied to harm to neighbours' outlook and privacy, not only to character and appearance (DL ¶17, ¶42–44).
- P3 was read as covering daylight, sunlight and pollution, so it did not decide an outlook and privacy case (DL ¶18).
- A scheme can pass the HE6(4) balance and still fail DP3(3): the same benefits were "substantial" against heritage harm but gave no clear justification for the living-conditions harm (DL ¶37, ¶44).
- Meeting SPD separation distances "does not, in itself, demonstrate that a proposal would preserve neighbouring living conditions" (DL ¶10).
- The letter applies S5(1)(d) and S5(2) to a Green Belt site rather than S5(5); the balance and the trigger are the same under either route, so the outcome is unaffected (DL ¶39, ¶41, ¶45).
PINS-6011321:
## Summary
A retrospective storage building in Kippax, built on part of the car park approved for three new houses, was dismissed on highway safety. The remaining parking layout did not work, and vehicles serving the store would be pushed to an access with restricted visibility. That harm, contrary to TR6 and given significant weight, substantially outweighed the limited benefit of reusing developed land under S4. The building's appearance was acceptable.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I have considered the revised Framework in determining this appeal" (DL ¶4).
- **Highway safety, TR6: FAIL.** "Even a small increase would have unacceptable road safety implications, bringing vehicles into greater conflict with passing traffic and increasing the risk of accidents" (DL ¶12). "the proposed development has an unacceptable adverse impact on highway safety in relation to access and car parking provision" (DL ¶13).
- **Off-site parking.** "As this land lies outside the applicant's control, a condition requiring reliance upon these nearby parking areas would be unreasonable" (DL ¶8).
- **Character, DP3: accord.** "It is also compliant with Policy BE1 of the Kippax Neighbourhood Plan and Policy DP3 of the Framework" (DL ¶17).

## Planning balance
S4(1). For: use of previously developed land, limited weight because it "occupies part of the approved car park to the neighbouring residential terrace rather than wholly vacant or underutilised land" (DL ¶19). Against: "This harm would be long lasting and is contrary to Policy TR6 of the Framework. I therefore attach significant weight to this harm" (DL ¶20). "the benefits of granting planning permission are substantially outweighed by adverse effects" (DL ¶21). The S4(2)(c) trigger is not expressly used.

## What made the difference
The store took the visitor parking of the neighbouring terrace and left a layout that failed even on the appellant's own swept paths. A nil accident record did not answer a new source of movements at a poor access.

## Transferable points
- An "unacceptable" highway safety impact under TR6 can come from a small increase in movements at an access with restricted visibility, despite a clean accident record (DL ¶12–13).
- Parking on land outside the red line and the appellant's control cannot be secured by condition (DL ¶8).
- The benefit of reusing developed land is limited where the land is in active use as approved parking (DL ¶19).
PINS-6011337:
## Summary
Three large over-55s houses at the edge of the small village of Glentham were dismissed. The council has a five-year supply and a recent local plan, which the inspector gave full weight. The appellant's evidence of a general shortage of housing for older people did not show a need for large four-bedroom houses in this location, so no S5(1) category was met and S5(4) applied. The scheme harmed the approach to the village, was poorly connected, and was at so low a density that L3(4) said it should be refused.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** The parties had the opportunity to comment on the 2026 Framework (DL ¶17).
- **Development plan.** "The continuous built form of the settlement clearly ends at the current extent of the Sunnyside houses on this side of the A631." (DL ¶8).
- **Need must be type-specific.** "The evidence presented does not indicate how much, or if any part of the numeric need for market age exclusive accommodation, would relate to large 4-bedroom dwellings, particularly in an edge of a small rural settlement location." (DL ¶10).
- **Plan weight (Annex A ¶2): KEPT.** "it is not considered that the LP is inconsistent with the Framework with regard to Policies S1, S4 or S23 and can be afforded full weight" (DL ¶18).
- **Plan-making policies.** "This is a matter for the review of the LP which is already underway. This will be required to take into account the plan making Polices HO1 and HO5 of the Framework referred to by the appellant. This does not reduce the primacy of the development plan at this time." (DL ¶19).
- **S5(1)(e): FAIL.** "This proposal does not represent infill development as suggested by the appellant as it extends development away from the settlement." (DL ¶21).
- **S5(1)(j): FAIL.** "There is no unmet need for housing in general." (DL ¶22).
- **Location, TR3(1)(a): FAIL.** "as no evidence has been provided with regard to bus frequency, it cannot be assumed that a convenient service would be available" (DL ¶23). "The Connectivity Tool provides a particularly low score for connectivity. Whilst it is positive with regard to comparisons with other local sites and rural villages, it reflects the physical situation on the ground, including the local absence of services and the need to travel to access them." (DL ¶24).
- **Housing, HO7: moderate.** "As need has not been established, either generally or with regard to this specific form of specialist housing, only moderate weight is afforded to the additional provision of housing" (DL ¶28).
- **Density, L3: FAIL.** "It therefore conflicts with Framework Policy L3(2b) which requires that development footprints should make the best use of a site’s development potential. In these circumstances, the policy indicates that the development should be refused." (DL ¶29).

## Planning balance
Plan-led, with the plan at full weight (DL ¶31). The Framework is then taken as a material consideration: "Policy L3(4) is clear that development proposals that do not make efficient use of land should be refused" and "there are no exceptional circumstances that indicate that the benefits of the proposal would substantially outweigh the adverse effects" (DL ¶32). Moderate weight to three homes against landscape harm, a TR3 conflict and an L3 conflict.

## What made the difference
A council with a five-year supply and a 2023 plan. Without a shortfall, S5(1)(j) depended on evidence of need for this particular product, and a district-wide count of older people's housing did not show it. Type-specific evidence of need for large accessible houses in small villages, or a site within the village's developed footprint, would have been needed; the low density would still have had to be justified.

## Transferable points
- Where the council has a five-year supply, S5(1)(j) "evidenced unmet need" must be shown for the type of housing proposed, including its size and location; a numeric district-wide deficit is not enough (DL ¶10, ¶13, ¶22).
- HO7 weight falls to moderate where need is not established (DL ¶28).
- A plan that addresses older people's housing through a general mix policy is not materially inconsistent with the Framework and keeps full weight (DL ¶18).
- HO1 and HO5 are plan-making policies; a rise in local housing need since adoption is a matter for the plan review, not a reason to reduce the plan's weight (DL ¶19).
- L3(2)(b) was applied to an unallocated site outside a settlement, and L3(4) treated as a refusal policy for very low density (DL ¶29, ¶32).
- A bus stop without evidence of frequency does not show a genuine choice of transport modes (DL ¶23).
- A Connectivity Tool score that is good only by comparison with other rural places is still a low score (DL ¶24).
- HO9(1)(a) can count against specialist housing for older people in a poorly connected location even where the accessibility standard is met (DL ¶26-27).
PINS-6011602:
## Summary
An external metal staircase giving a first-floor flat access to the rear garden of a Victorian terrace in Brent was allowed. The inspector found it narrow, lightweight and discreetly sited against the outrigger, so it would not harm the host property or the area, and it accorded with local Policy DMP1 and the design policies of the Framework.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I am satisfied, however, that the relevant policy position for this appeal is not materially different and that its publication has not prejudiced any party" (DL ¶2).
- **Design: accord.** "The Framework seeks development that is sympathetic to local character, while not preventing or discouraging appropriate innovation or change" (DL ¶6). This is the December 2024 wording; the slip is incidental, as no harm was found.
- **No harm.** "the absence of similar features in the vicinity does not in itself mean that a proposal would cause harm" (DL ¶9).

## What made the difference
The staircase could not be seen from the street, sat below the eaves in a side passage, and would be read against rear elevations that already vary.

## Transferable points
- Novelty is not harm: a feature absent from neighbouring properties is assessed on its own effect (DL ¶9).
- Precedent arguments carry little weight where acceptability turns on site-specific siting (DL ¶13).
PINS-6012098:
## Summary
A JOLT electric vehicle charge point with advertising screens on the Old Brompton Road footway was dismissed, with its linked advertisement appeal. It would harm the setting of the Boltons Conservation Area at the lower level, and the modest public benefits did not outweigh that harm under HE6(4). Unlike the sister case at Fulham Road (PINS-6012105), it also failed on highway safety, because pedestrians naturally walked across the proposed position where the footway narrows.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties have been consulted and provided with an opportunity to provide comments on it in relation to these appeals" (DL ¶4).
- **Heritage: harm to one conservation area, none to the other.** "I do not find harm in relation to this aspect and the setting of the Thurloe/Smiths Charity CA would be preserved" (DL ¶12).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "Whilst the degree of harm resulting from the proposed JOLT and advertisement on the significance of the Boltons CA would be at the lower level, in accordance with Policy HE6 (4) of the Framework, that harm should be weighed against any public benefits of the proposals" (DL ¶13). "I find insufficient public benefits arising from the proposals to offset the identified harm to which I attach substantial weight" (DL ¶15).
- **Highway safety: harm.** "I observed many pedestrians naturally move out to the edge of the pavement and across the position of the proposed JOLT which formed a natural desire line for pedestrians in this location" (DL ¶19). The unit "would cause an undue obstruction to pedestrians and impede the free flow of pedestrian movements, including those with mobility impairments" (DL ¶20).

## Planning balance
HE6(4): lower-level harm to a conservation area's setting against modest public benefits. No S4 balance is run; the conclusion is plan-led (DL ¶26).

## What made the difference
Two things: the open footway within 30 m of the Boltons Conservation Area, and the pinch point next door that pushed pedestrians across the proposed position. Meeting the 2 m numerical guidance did not answer what the inspector saw on site.

## Transferable points
- Compliance with a minimum clear footway width does not settle pedestrian safety where the footway narrows nearby and the unit would sit on an observed desire line (DL ¶19–20).
- Setting harm was found for a conservation area about 30 m away but not for one about 70 m away behind intervening buildings (DL ¶11–12).
- Lower-level harm to a conservation area's setting outweighs the benefits of one public charge point (DL ¶13–15).
PINS-6012105:
## Summary
A JOLT electric vehicle charge point with double-sided advertising screens on the Fulham Road footway was dismissed, with its linked advertisement appeal. The unit would be the most prominent feature in an open, uncluttered footway and would harm the setting of the Thurloe/Smiths Charity Conservation Area at the lower level. The public benefits of on-street charging were modest and achievable less harmfully, so they did not outweigh the harm under HE6(4). Pedestrian safety was acceptable.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The main parties have been consulted and provided with an opportunity to provide comments on it in relation to these appeals" (DL ¶4).
- **Character: harm.** "it would have an undue presence in its setting, appearing as an incongruous and uncharacteristic feature" (DL ¶9).
- **HE6(4): FAIL.** "Whilst the degree of harm resulting from the proposed JOLT and advertisement on the significance of the CA would be at the lower level, in accordance with Policy HE6 (4) of the Framework, that harm should be weighed against any public benefits of the proposals" (DL ¶12). "I find insufficient public benefits arising from the proposals to offset the identified harm to which I attach substantial weight" (DL ¶14).
- **Less harmful alternatives.** The benefits would be modest and "there is no indication that they could not be achieved in a less harmful manner than proposed" (DL ¶25).
- **Highway safety: acceptable.** The unit "would not have any additional significant impact in this respect and would, in my view, leave ample room for the free and safe movement of pedestrians" (DL ¶19).

## Planning balance
HE6(4): lower-level harm to a conservation area's setting against modest public benefits. No S4 balance is run; the conclusion is that the scheme is "not in accordance with the development plan when read as a whole" (DL ¶26).

## What made the difference
The open, lightly furnished footway opposite the conservation area. A unit replacing existing street furniture, as with the BT Street Hub the appellant cited, would have been judged against a different baseline.

## Transferable points
- Lower-level harm to a conservation area's setting from a single item of street furniture outweighs the benefits of one public charge point (DL ¶12–14).
- Benefits that could be achieved "in a less harmful manner" are discounted in the HE6(4) balance (DL ¶25).
- A footway width just below a council's SPD standard is not harmful where the unit does not interrupt a pedestrian desire line (DL ¶18–19).
PINS-6012202:
## Summary
Permission in principle for up to two dwellings replacing kennel buildings in the countryside near Weeton was allowed. The scheme conflicted with the local plan's countryside policy and future occupiers would rely heavily on cars. But the site is previously developed land, so S5(1)(d) applied, and the inspector held that (d) does not require a site to be well-related to a settlement. The local countryside policy, which has no equivalent provision, was given very limited weight. Housing had substantial weight, undiminished by the small scale, and the moderate transport harm did not substantially outweigh it.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** No switch paragraph. The letter cites the "National Planning Policy Framework 2026" and its policy codes (DL ¶13).
- **Location and access, TR3: HARM (moderate).** "There is no continuous lit footpath to Weeton or the nearest bus stop." (DL ¶10). "future occupiers would have a heavy reliance on private vehicles to access services and facilities" but "driving distances would be short to both Weeton and the larger settlement of Wesham, moderating the extent of harm" (DL ¶11).
- **Plan weight (Annex A ¶2): CUT.** "Policy GD4 of the Local Plan is more restrictive than the criteria in Policy S5 of the Framework and does not have similar provisions relating to the development of previously developed land (PDL) outside of settlements. As such, I give Policy GD4, and by connection Policy S1 in relation to this matter, very limited weight." (DL ¶13).
- **S5(1)(d): PASS.** "Criterion d) of Policy S5 does not require that proposals for the redevelopment of PDL are physically well-related to a settlement, as that requirement only appears within criterions h) and j), with no indication that it is to be applied to the other forms of development listed." (DL ¶15).
- **Housing, HO7: substantial.** "The modest scale of the development does not diminish the weight I give these benefits." (DL ¶16).
- **Weight of the transport harm.** "the adverse effects in terms of accessibility to services and facilities and in seeking to guide development towards sustainable locations carry no more than moderate weight" (DL ¶19).

## Planning balance
S5(1) with the S5(2) check: "There are no relevant national decision-making policies which indicate that the proposal should be specifically refused. As such, when considered collectively, the benefits of the development would not be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects." (DL ¶20). Substantial weight to two homes; moderate weight to the TR3 conflict; limited weight to the loss of the business. Then section 38(6): "The proposed development would conflict with the development plan but material considerations, namely the provisions of the Framework, indicate that a decision should be made other than in accordance with it." (DL ¶23).

## What made the difference
The site's status as previously developed land. That opened S5(1)(d), cut the weight of the countryside policy that would otherwise have barred the scheme, and led the inspector to hold the transport harm to moderate weight because the Framework supports the location in principle. The existing business's own traffic also reduced the net effect. On a greenfield site the same route and distances would have been tested under S5(4).

## Transferable points
- S5(1)(d) has no "well-related to a settlement" test; that requirement appears only in (h) and (j) (DL ¶15).
- A local countryside policy with no provision for redeveloping previously developed land outside settlements is more restrictive than S5 and gets very limited weight under Annex A ¶2; transport policies in line with TR3 keep their weight (DL ¶13).
- A TR3 conflict is weighed in the S5(1) balance and was not treated as a refusal policy; where S5 supports the location in principle the inspector held it to moderate weight (DL ¶18-20).
- Trips generated by the existing use of previously developed land moderate the transport harm of its redevelopment (DL ¶11).
- HO7 substantial weight was given in full to two homes at permission in principle stage, where the council has a shortfall (DL ¶16).
- Appeal decisions made under the previous Framework can be distinguished on that ground alone (DL ¶21).
PINS-6012344:
## Summary
Change of use of a closed bar next to Greenwich Station to a convenience store was allowed, in a joint letter with a linked appeal for a cafe (PINS-6012348). The inspector found the last use was a drinking establishment with expanded food provision, not a public house, so the London Plan and local pub-protection policies did not decide the case. Under Framework policy HC6(1)(c) there was sufficient alternative provision of drinking establishments in the town centre.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The parties have been provided with the opportunity to comment on the implications of the revisions to their cases" (DL ¶3).
- **Is it a public house?** "on the balance of probabilities, the last use of No 189 constitutes a drinking establishment with expanded food provision" (DL ¶16). The pub policies "are not wholly determinative for this appeal given that I have found No 189 to not be a public house" (DL ¶17).
- **Night-time economy (London Plan HC6): accord.** "there remains limited evidence before me to adequately demonstrate that the loss of a drinking establishment in this location would result in unacceptable harm to the overall night-time economy and vitality of Greenwich’s Town Centre" (DL ¶20).
- **Framework HC6(1)(c): PASS.** "I am satisfied that there is sufficient alternative provision of drinking establishments in the local area, such that the loss of the drinking … establishment as part of the appeal schemes would not diminish access to key community facilities and public service infrastructure" (DL ¶25; the break is a page break).
- **Heritage: no harm.** "the appeal proposals would preserve the setting of both Greenwich Station and Queen Elizabeth’s Almshouses" (DL ¶28).

## Planning balance
None needed. The scheme complied with London Plan Policy HC6 and Framework HC6(1)(c), and "The material considerations do not indicate that a decision should be made other than in accordance with the development plan" (DL ¶43).

## What made the difference
The classification of the last use. Because the premises had traded as a bar with food rather than a public house, the stricter marketing tests in the London Plan, the local plan (two years) and Framework HC6(1)(a) (12 months) were not applied, and the plentiful supply of other drinking establishments nearby met HC6(1)(c).

## Transferable points
- HC6(1)(a) to (c) are alternatives: sufficient alternative provision under (c) was enough without marketing evidence under (a) (DL ¶9–10, ¶25).
- A drinking establishment was treated as a key community facility for HC6, and the alternative-provision test was met by other drinking establishments in the same town centre (DL ¶25).
- Development plan policies that protect "public houses" do not decide a case about a bar with expanded food provision; what the last use was is a matter of judgement on the evidence (DL ¶14–17).
- New marketing evidence produced at appeal may be refused where interested parties have not seen it (DL ¶6).
PINS-6012348:
## Summary
Appeal B of a joint letter: change of use of a closed bar next to Greenwich Station to a cafe, allowed alongside Appeal A for a convenience store (PINS-6012344, which has the fuller analysis). The reasoning is common to both: the last use was not a public house, and Framework policy HC6(1)(c) was met by other drinking establishments in the town centre.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I have taken account of the revised Framework, and any comments made, in my determination of both appeal ‘A’ and appeal ‘B’" (DL ¶3).
- **Night-time economy.** "the proposed use of No 189 as a café would help diversify the range of night-time activities" (DL ¶23).
- **Framework HC6(1)(c): PASS.** "Accordingly, the appeal schemes would accord with Policy HC6(1)(C) of the Framework" (DL ¶25).
- **Conclusion on the main issue.** "the appeal schemes in both appeal ‘A’ and appeal ‘B’ would not result in the loss of a pub and nor would it unacceptably harm the night-time economy of Greenwich Town Centre" (DL ¶26).

## What made the difference
As for Appeal A: the classification of the last use as a bar with food rather than a public house, and the number of other drinking establishments nearby. For the cafe, the London Plan's support for extending the hours of daytime uses added to the case.

## Transferable points
- A cafe replacing a bar can be treated as diversifying night-time activity under the London Plan (DL ¶21, ¶23).
- A condition on extraction equipment can be limited to new or materially altered equipment where the existing use raised no amenity concern (DL ¶41).
PINS-6001859:
## Summary
A restaurant on More London Place, Southwark, sought a larger outdoor seating area enclosed by a 2.8 m pergola, glazed screens, planters and an awning. The inspector found no harm to the settings of the Tooley Street Conservation Area or Grade I Tower Bridge, but held that the structure would be incongruous in the cohesive contemporary frontage. That conflict with DP3(1) lacked clear justification, so the S4(2) trigger applied and the modest benefits were substantially outweighed. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The parties were invited to comment on the revised Framework, and I have taken account of the comments received" (DL ¶2).
- **Heritage settings: NO HARM.** "there would be no harm caused to the significance of these designated heritage assets as a result of this proposal within their settings" (DL ¶14).
- **Design, DP3(1): CONFLICT.** "the development would have an incongruous appearance, and it would be harmfully conspicuous in views from the walkway" (DL ¶16). "It follows that there would be conflict with Policy DP3(1) of the Framework, which expects proposals to respond to their context, and to integrate with and enhance their surroundings" (DL ¶17).
- **Benefits.** TC2 substantial weight is "relevant here" (DL ¶22), but "the social and economic benefits that would arise from the proposed development would be modest, and this limits the weight that they carry in this case" (DL ¶23).
- **DP3(3) / S4(2)(c): FAIL.** "In my judgement, the scheme lacks clear justification and its benefits would be substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶24). The letter cites "Policy S4(2)(a)(c)", a slip for S4(2)(c).

## Planning balance
S4 (inside a settlement). The design harm was routed through DP3(3) and the S4(2) trigger, then set against modest leisure and economic benefits. Conclusion framed plan-led: conflict with the development plan as a whole and no material consideration indicating otherwise (DL ¶25).

## What made the difference
The size and permanence of the enclosure against a sleek, cohesive frontage where alfresco seating is otherwise loose, low furniture. The heritage objection fell away because the structure sits in line with an existing advertisement screen and keeps the central views to Tower Bridge. A lighter, lower structure aligned with the tall ground-floor windows might have passed.

## Transferable points
- A DP3(1) conflict, found to lack clear justification, engages S4(2)(c) and makes the benefits substantially outweighed. This is the full DP3(3) route in a short letter (DL ¶17, ¶24).
- TC2's substantial weight to town-centre vitality does not attach in full to modest benefits from a single premises (DL ¶22–23).
- Setting harm depends on whether the scheme interrupts the views through which the setting is experienced (DL ¶14).
PINS-6001939:
## Summary
Listed building consent for a through-floor lift in Adsdean House, a Grade II listed house in the South Downs National Park. The lift would cut through a c.1900 ceiling and floor and seal two doors. The inspector graded the harm as low but gave it "considerable importance and weight", found the informal public benefits and the appellant's access needs worth only modest weight, and dismissed the appeal.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "The Council and the appellant have had opportunity to comment on this and I have taken into account any representations received" (DL ¶3).
- **Significance of later fabric.** "The siting of the lift would be within a non-original later addition to the property. Nevertheless, given its age and history of this part of the property, it contributes positively to the evolution and architectural phasing of the building" (DL ¶10).
- **HE6(3): HARM, low.** "I find the harm to the heritage asset to be, at a low level of harm but nevertheless is of considerable importance and weight" (DL ¶13).
- **Public benefits: modest.** Tours and community meetings are "done on an informal ad-hoc basis, and as such, there is no guarantee of this continuing in any formal manner" (DL ¶14).
- **HE6(4) / HE4(2): FAIL.** "in giving considerable importance and weight to the harm to the significance of this designated heritage asset, I find that this would not be outweighed by the public benefits that the proposal would generate" (DL ¶17); the harm "has not been supported by clear and convincing justification" (DL ¶18).
- **Reversibility condition rejected** as not precise enough (DL ¶15).

## Planning balance
HE6(4) harm against public benefits, with HE6(1) substantial weight to conservation and HE6(3) considerable weight to the harm stated correctly (DL ¶17). Personal access needs under the PSED counted as modest (DL ¶23).

## What made the difference
The lift took historic fabric from a part of the house that is not original but is still part of its evolution, and the public benefits were informal and unsecured. Evidence that no less harmful route to the upper floor existed, or secured public access, might have tipped the balance.

## Transferable points
- Later, non-original parts of a listed building can still carry significance through its "evolution and architectural phasing" (DL ¶10).
- Informal, ad hoc public access is not a secured public benefit and gets modest weight (DL ¶14).
- A reversibility condition fails if it cannot say when reinstatement is triggered (DL ¶15).
PINS-6004363:
## Summary
A BT Street Hub with two 75-inch digital screens on a pedestrianised Folkestone town-centre pavement, in the setting of the Leas and Bayle Conservation Area. The planning appeal and the joint advert appeal (6004364) were both dismissed. The hub would be prominent and intrusive, causing modest harm to the CA through its setting; connectivity and kiosk-removal benefits were small or limited. The letter runs DP3(3) through S4(2)(c) with an explicit clear-justification finding.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I sought the views of the parties on the implications of the new Framework on the appeal" (DL ¶7).
- **Character and CA setting: HARM.** "Modest harm to the significance of the CA through its setting would therefore arise" (DL ¶15).
- **CO1: small benefit.** "In these circumstances and due to the limited scale of the development this amounts to a small benefit" (DL ¶17).
- **HE4(2) / HE6(4): FAIL.** "the public benefits are insufficient to provide such justification and outweigh the identified harm to the significance of the CA through its setting" (DL ¶19).
- **Plan weight (Transitional(2)).** HB1 and RL9 "are consistent with section 14 of the Framework in seeking to achieve well-design places, in particular Policy DP3. On this basis the identified conflict with these policies carries significant weight" (DL ¶26).
- **DP3(3) via S4(2)(c): FAIL.** "Based on my findings, there are no clear justifications for the harm. The benefits of approving the development are therefore substantially outweighed by the adverse effects" (DL ¶28).

## Planning balance
Plan-led (s38(6)) with S4 applied: conflict with HB1/RL9 at significant weight; DP3(3) conflict without clear justification engages S4(2)(c), so benefits substantially outweighed (DL ¶27–29). HE6(4) run separately first (DL ¶16–19).

## What made the difference
The hub's height, solid form and large double-sided screens at a crossroads, visible in long views into the CA, against benefits that were not shown to meet any local deficiency. The small-scale CO1 benefit was reduced because no coverage gap was evidenced (DL ¶17). An evidenced coverage deficiency, or a less prominent position, might have shifted the HE6(4) balance.

## Transferable points
- CO1's substantial weight can shrink to "a small benefit" where there is no evidence of local deficiency in the services offered (DL ¶17).
- Kiosk removal and the Universal Service Obligation carry limited weight where not shown to require this specific location (DL ¶18).
- Clear DP3(3) sequence: DP3(1) conflict, "no clear justifications for the harm", therefore S4(2) — benefits substantially outweighed (DL ¶27–28).
PINS-6004526:
## Summary
Outline permission for two bungalows with rooms in the roof, on a strip of former grassland beside 147 Eastcote Lane, Harrow. The Council refused on privacy and biodiversity net gain (BNG). The inspector found obscure-glazed, fixed-shut dormers removed any overlooking, and that although garden-based habitat gains could not count, off-site units or credits made the statutory BNG condition capable of discharge. Allowed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "the parties have had the opportunity to comment on the changes in relation to this appeal" (DL ¶6).
- **Privacy: no harm.** The Framework point was set aside: "the revised Framework has altered its approach and does not now refer to amenity in a general sense as it previously did but rather it now refers to amenity in some specific areas. I do not find reference to the Framework to be strictly applicable in the particular circumstances of this appeal" (DL ¶14).
- **BNG baseline.** "I reach the same conclusion as the Council that the baseline condition is grassland" (DL ¶19).
- **Garden habitat.** "where post-development gardens are private and have no public access, biodiversity net gains cannot be legally secured" (DL ¶24). "The mandatory 10% BNG could not therefore be secured on the site" (DL ¶25).
- **Discharge route.** Off-site creation or statutory credits are "a realistic and achievable alternative to onsite gains. Accordingly, this provides sufficient certainty that the biodiversity gain condition is capable of being successfully discharged" (DL ¶26). Accords with N2 (DL ¶27).
- **Permitted development rights (DM6).** "conditions should not be used to restrict national permitted development rights unless there is clear justification to do so" (DL ¶35); the Council's suggested restrictions were omitted.

## Planning balance
Plan-led: no conflict with the development plan on either main issue, "having had regard to the development plan as a whole, the appeal is allowed" (DL ¶37). No S4 balance was run.

## What made the difference
The fixed obscure glazing removed the privacy objection, and the inspector read the BNG test as whether the statutory condition is capable of discharge, not whether on-site gains are proven. The Council's own later approval of a near-identical scheme also shaped the conditions.

## Transferable points
- The 2026 Framework no longer has a general amenity policy; one inspector did not find a Framework-based general amenity refusal "strictly applicable" (DL ¶14).
- Private gardens cannot count towards mandatory BNG, but a scheme can still pass if off-site units or credits are realistic (DL ¶24-26).
- DM6: conditions removing PD rights need clear justification (DL ¶35).
PINS-6004640:
## Summary
A farmstead in the South Downs National Park sought a three-bay garage and a permanent version of an access track first built as a temporary construction access under permitted development. The garage was acceptable, but the track cut through former woodland and brought vehicle movements into a tranquil area. The inspector found significant landscape and tranquillity harm contrary to N4 and the park's local plan. Dismissed.

## Issues and findings
- **Transition.** "I have not sought comments from the main parties in respect of the revisions to the Framework as I do not consider the policy emphasis regarding the main issue in this case to have changed" (DL ¶3).
- **Access track, N4: FAIL.** "Landscape harms arising from the proposal would be significant" (DL ¶12). The permitted-development track "only lasts for the duration of the construction period, and the provision is explicitly worded to prevent a precedent for permanent development" (DL ¶13). "the proposed development would not conserve or enhance the landscape within which it sits" (DL ¶17). ¶19 calls the same harm "substantial harm to the character and appearance of the area".
